+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 75.7
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The transfer vessel's air filtration system hummed with a persistent mechanical drone, a sound Arthur Neegan had long since learned to associate with the particular flavor of recycled atmosphere that filled the space between worlds. It was a thin, metallic taste, a ghost of the oxygen it had once been, now stripped and respun a thousand times over. He sat in a utilitarian crash-cushion bolted to the bulkhead, the stark white light of the overhead strips reflecting off the polished metal of the walls. He felt small, a piece of gear himself, catalogued and stored. Across the narrow compartment, a woman in a severe charcoal-grey uniform with the stylized crimson spider of the Antares Diplomatic Corp on her collar stood with perfect stillness. Her name, she had offered without prompting, was Envoy Kaelen. Her politeness was the most unnerving thing about her. It was the politeness of a locked door. "Your comfort is our priority, Mr. Neegan," she had said when they had boarded. "We trust the journey has been satisfactory." He had merely nodded. His own home, a dome of reinforced plexi-steel and Martian brick he'd helped lay himself, now felt like a memory from another man's life. The docking clamps of the transfer vessel engaged with a shudder that ran through the deck plates. A series of soft chimes echoed. "We have arrived," Kaelen said, her voice as level as the horizon. "If you will follow me." The airlock opened not onto the bustling, sweat-and-red-dust atmosphere of a Martian port, but into a silent, cavernous bay. The ship they were on was a shuttle, he realized. This was the true vessel. The air here was different—cooler, cleaner, and carrying a faint, unfamiliar ozone tang. The floor was a dark, seamless composite that swallowed the sound of their boots. Armed guards in the same charcoal uniforms flanked the bay exit, their faces impassive. Kaelen led him down a wide corridor. The walls were adorned not with art, but with star-charts, each system glowing with a soft, internal light. One, larger than the rest, dominated a junction. It showed a web of routes radiating from a single point labeled SOL, with thick, pulsing lines of red connecting it to a cluster of systems he vaguely knew as the Antares Arm. "An impressive map," Arthur said, his voice sounding rough in the refined silence. "It is a logistical chart, Mr. Neegan," Kaelen replied without turning. "It illustrates energy expenditure and cargo tonnage across the primary trade corridors. The balance is... delicate." She stopped before a set of sliding double doors, which opened into a large, semi-circular room. A vast viewport curved along the wall, offering a breathtaking, silent vista of Mars. From this high orbit, the planet was a serene marble of rust and cream, the great canyons mere scratches, the settlements invisible. A man stood before it, his back to them. He was tall, dressed not in uniform but in a simple, impeccably tailored tunic of dark blue. "Envoy Kaelen. Thank you for your efficient service." His voice was calm, cultured, and it carried easily across the room. He turned. He was older, with a face that seemed more accustomed to chessboards than physical labor, yet his eyes were sharp and missed nothing. He was, Arthur thought, utterly and completely in control. "Mr. Neegan." He gestured to a pair of chairs that seemed to be made of molded crystal. "Please. My name is Corvan. I represent the interests of the Antares Compact. They are, for the moment, my interests." Arthur sat, the crystal cool beneath him. The chair was surprisingly comfortable. "My interests, sir, were in my claim and my home." "Ah, yes. The claim." Corvan moved to a low table between them. A map of the Valles Marineris region shimmered into existence in the air above it. A single, bright point pulsed over a network of lines Arthur knew intimately—the survey charts of his plot. "Nine hundred square kilometers of Martian commons, leased under standard terraformer's tenure. Unremarkable. Until, of course, you bored a probe into what you thought was a nickel-iron anomaly." The point on the map flared, and a cascade of data streamed beside it. Isotopic signatures. Decay-rate graphs. Energy output projections that climbed into numbers that didn't seem real. "I followed standard survey protocol," Arthur said, his voice tight. "You did," Corvan agreed mildly. "And in so doing, you located the single largest confirmed deposit of Azra-7 outside the Kuiper Belt. You have, in effect, found a continent. And on that continent, you have built a house. The ownership of the house is not in question. The ownership of the continent is what brings us here." He leaned forward, his elbows on his knees. "The corporations are coming, Mr. Neegan. You know this. Globex, Martian Mineral, Krasny—they will offer you sums. Vast, unimaginable sums. They will also offer you an end. To your freedom. To your life. An accident in a pressure lock. A 'mechanical failure' in a deep bore. They are not subtle, but they are effective. You would become a footnote in a corporate prospectus." The air in the room seemed to grow thinner. "The Antares Compact," Corvan continued, "is not a mining corporation. We are a coalition of systems, with a vested interest in... stability. Interstellar drives and weapons built from uncontrolled Azra will shatter the current balance. A balance that has kept the lanes open and the wars cold for a century." "So you're offering me protection," Arthur said, the words tasting like ash. "I am offering you a role," Corvan corrected. "We will fund you. You will retain a controlling interest in your claim—far more than any corporation would allow. We will provide the technology, the security. You will be the legal owner, the face of the enterprise. The Azra will be mined under our long-term, strategic guidance. It will be used to fuel the next generation of interstellar engines for the Compact—engines that will bring new worlds into the fold, expand the market for Martian produce and manufactured goods, and ensure humanity's future is not constrained to one fragile system. In short, Mr. Neegan, I am offering you the chance to be the father of the Second Expansion, and to become the wealthiest man in the Sol system in the bargain." Arthur stared out the viewport at his home planet. "And if I refuse? If I take the corporate money?" Corvan's smile did not reach his eyes. "Then you will be a very rich man for a very short time. And the Compact will achieve its ends through other, less pleasant means. We are patient. The question is not whether the Azra is controlled, Mr. Neegan. The question is by whom, and for what purpose. And I am offering you a purpose grander than a line item on a quarterly report." The hum of the ship's filtration system was the only sound. Arthur looked from Corvan's unwavering gaze to the silent guard at the door, from the serene face of Mars to the stark, logical beauty of the star-chart on the wall. He was a first-generation settler. A man who built things in the dirt. But he understood the immutable law that governed the dirt, and the stars, and everything in between. Power, once consolidated, never disperses willingly. "What," Arthur Neegan asked, his voice quiet but clear as a drill-bit hitting stone, "does the Antares Compact intend to do with the most dangerous substance in the galaxy?" Corvan's smile widened a fraction. "Now," he said, his voice a purr, "you are asking the right questions."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter competently executes the brief: it opens aboard the transfer vessel, features the Antares diplomatic corp, delivers a dialogue-heavy meeting with an offer, and plants intrigue. The prose is clean and controlled, with some effective imagery (the star-charts, the viewport of Mars, "the politeness of a locked door"). Corvan is a serviceable Asimovian antagonist-negotiator, and the geopolitical stakes are sketched efficiently. However, the piece leans on familiar tropes—the omniscient, silky-voiced envoy, the "join us or die" ultimatum—and the ending line ("you are asking the right questions") is a cliché. Arthur is thin; his settler background is stated rather than felt. The dialogue is polished but occasionally expository, with Corvan delivering world-building monologues. The Asimovian big-picture/small-picture contrast (power politics vs. one man's claim) is present but somewhat on-the-nose. Length is appropriate. Overall a solid, professional pastiche that lacks the conceptual surprise of Asimov's best work. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 74.1
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The only light is a deep, arterial red. It turns the darkroom into a kind of womb, a space outside of time where things can gestate before being born into the harsh light of the world. For the past three hours, this has been our universe: me, Elliot, and the acrid tang of fixer in the air. Usually, I’m the one in charge. In the studio, in my critiques, in my relationships. I have a vision, and I bend the world, and the people in it, to fit. But Elliot has always been an exception. He’s a quiet country I haven’t figured out how to colonize. He’s nineteen, all sharp angles and soft edges, a walking contradiction in thrifted black. Tonight, he’s wearing a faded Bauhaus t-shirt under a velvet blazer, his eyeliner smudged just so. He’s beautiful in a way that defies easy categorization, and for a semester, that mystery has been a low hum under my skin. Our final project, a series on “liminal states,” has given me a reason to get closer. The late nights are a necessary evil, but I’ve been craving them. The red light is a confessional. It flattens everyone, makes us equals in the dark. “Hand me that beaker, would you?” I ask, my voice feeling too loud in the quiet. He passes it, his fingers brushing mine. A spark, tiny but definite. He pulls back quickly, focusing on the print emerging in the developer tray. It’s a photo of him, actually. I’d taken it last week, his face half-shadowed, his expression unreadable. He’d agreed, a little shyly, when I’d asked. “It’s weird, seeing yourself like this,” he murmurs, his voice a soft counterpoint to the gentle sloshing of chemicals. “So… exposed.” “That’s the point, isn’t it?” I say, trying to keep my tone light, professional. But my eyes are on the way the red light catches in his dark hair, turning it the color of dried blood. “Liminal. The space between.” He’s quiet for a long moment, just watching his own image slowly ghost into existence. The silence stretches, becoming thick and meaningful. This is it, I think. The air has been charged for weeks, full of unspoken things. “Can I… can I tell you something, Dani?” he finally asks, not looking at me. “Always.” The word is out before I can vet it, too earnest. He takes a shaky breath. “I’ve been thinking a lot about this project. The in-between spaces.” He gestures vaguely at the trays, the hanging prints. “And I think… I think I live in one.” My assertive instincts flare up, a knee-jerk desire to define it for him, to say *I know, I see you*. I bite my tongue. This isn’t about me. “I don’t know what I am,” he says, the words barely a whisper. “Sometimes I look in the mirror, and the guy looking back… he doesn’t fit. It’s like wearing a suit that’s the wrong size. And other times… I don’t want to be a guy at all. I just want to be… me. But I don’t know what that looks like.” The confession hangs in the red air between us, fragile and terrifying. My heart does a complicated lurch—not pity, not exactly. It’s a fierce, protective sort of excitement. I’m witnessing the first tremor of a seismic shift, and I’m the only one here. My usual take-charge energy feels clumsy, like trying to perform surgery with a hammer. I want to wrap him in my arms and tell him it’s all going to be okay, but that feels possessive. I want to ask a dozen questions, but that feels like an interrogation. So I just nod, even though he’s not looking at me. “Thank you for telling me.” He finally risks a glance, his eyes wide and dark in the crimson gloom. He looks terrified of my reaction. I give him a small, genuine smile. “For what it’s worth,” I add, my voice softer than I intended, “I’ve always thought your style was killer. It’s… authentically you. Whatever that means.” A slow blush creeps up his neck, visible even in the monochrome light. He offers a tentative smile back. “Thanks.” The chemistry shifts. It’s no longer just the unspoken tension of attraction; it’s the intimacy of a shared secret. I feel a strange confusion swirl inside me. I’ve always known what I like: confidence, definition. Men who are unapologetically men, women who are unapologetically women. Elliot is a question mark, and I find myself wanting to read every single line of him, to understand the grammar of his soul. It’s terrifying and exhilarating. I reach for a fresh sheet of photo paper from the box on the counter, my mind buzzing. I’m so distracted by the revelation, by the sudden, tender closeness, that my hand is clumsy. My elbow catches the edge of the box. It tips. A dozen sheets of pristine, light-sensitive paper spill out onto the floor, right into the narrow beam of light leaking from under the door. We both freeze. A collective gasp. “No,” I whisper, the word a puff of air. We stare at the fallen sheets. In the space of a second, their potential is gone. The light has scorched them, turning them a useless, mottled grey. They are ruined. Exposed. The metaphor is so loud it’s almost comical. A beat of silence, and then Elliot lets out a short, sharp laugh. It’s not a happy sound, but it’s not despairing either. It’s pure, unadulterated absurdity. “Well,” he says, looking from the dead paper to my face. “I guess that’s one way to make a statement on impermanence.” I stare at him, at the wry, sad curve of his mouth, and I start laughing too. It’s a release. The tension breaks, not with a climax, but with a shared, helpless giggle over a stupid mistake. “Shit,” I say, running a hand through my hair. “That was my fault. I’m so sorry, Elliot.” “It’s okay,” he says, his laughter subsiding. “We have more. And… it’s kind of poetic, right? Some things can’t handle the light too soon.” He’s looking right at me, and his meaning is clear. He’s the paper. His identity is the image, still developing in the chemical bath of his own mind. It’s not ready for the world yet. I nod, the urge to fix it, to *do* something, finally quieting down. All I can do is be here, in the dark with him, and wait. “Yeah,” I say, my voice steady. “It is.” He smiles, a real one this time, and the red light catches in his eyes, making them look like they hold all the secrets in the world. And for the first time, I’m not trying to figure him out. I’m just happy to be in the darkroom with him when the image finally appears.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a competent, well-structured piece that hits most of the prompt's beats: the darkroom confessional atmosphere, Elliot's tentative gender questioning, Dani's assertiveness complicated by protectiveness, and her confusion about her own attractions. The red-light setting is used effectively as both literal and symbolic space. Strengths: The voice is consistent and confident, first-person and appropriately assertive-with-cracks. The spilled photo paper incident is a good plot device—concrete, believable, and thematically resonant (exposure before readiness). Elliot's "Some things can't handle the light too soon" lands as a natural line of dialogue rather than authorial sermonizing. The pacing is tight; the piece doesn't meander and earns its quiet ending. Weaknesses: The prose occasionally overreaches. "A quiet country I haven't figured out how to colonize" is an odd, slightly uncomfortable metaphor for describing a person, and "the grammar of his soul" is the kind of phrase the piece elsewhere mocks. The narrator's self-aware line "The metaphor is so loud it's almost comical" is a double-edged choice—it's witty, but it also signals the author knew the symbolism was heavy-handed and leaned in anyway. Some telling creeps in: "It's terrifying and exhilarating," "My heart does a complicated lurch—not pity, not exactly." Dani's identity confusion is stated more than dramatized; a more surprising or specific rendering of her internal shift would have elevated it. The emotional beats are somewhat predictable—shy confession, supportive response, accidental levity, warm resolution. The ending is gentle and earned, but the overall arc is safe rather than surprising. Elliot remains somewhat idealized: soft, beautiful, articulate about his own confusion in ways that feel writerly rather than like a nervous 19-year-old. Still, the dialogue is mostly natural, the scene logic is coherent, and the piece achieves genuine tenderness without tipping into sentimentality. It's a solid B+ piece: skilled, controlled, but not transcendent. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 73.4
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The roar of the Vespa was a violation of the morning peace, a mechanical scream that cut through the tourist murmur near the Trevi Fountain. Ben, clutching a dog-eared copy of *Rome: A Historical Guide*, didn't hear it until the screech of brakes made him jump, his leather-soled Oxford shoes skidding on the cobblestones. The bike stopped inches from his knees. The rider, a woman with wild, dark curls escaping a helmet, didn't look apologetic. She looked annoyed. "*Ma che fai, cammini come una lumaca?*" she snapped, flipping up her visor. Her eyes were dark and sparking. "You walk like a snail? In the middle of the road?" Ben’s face flushed a deep, apologetic red. "I... I am so dreadfully sorry. I was just looking at the map. The Aqua Virgo aqueduct, you see, it’s supposedly—" "*Inglese?*" she interrupted, her tone softening a fraction into something like amused pity. "British, yes. Terribly sorry." She sighed, a dramatic, full-body gesture. "*Dio mio.* Another one." She killed the engine, the sudden silence deafening. Her bike was a battered cherry-red Vespa, its body a map of its own adventures. A long, jagged scratch ran along the right side, a violent slash of bare metal against the paint, like a scar from a forgotten battle. "Are you hurt?" she asked, her eyes scanning him with an efficiency that was more clinical than concerned. "No, no. Just my dignity, I think." He attempted a smile. "Ben. Ben Carter." She looked him up and down—the tweed jacket in the Roman sun, the earnest, flustered expression. A slow, mischievous grin spread across her face. "Alessandra. And you, Ben Carter, are in desperate need of a real tour." Before he could protest, she had grabbed his guidebook, deftly plucking it from his fingers. She didn't hand it back. "This," she said, tapping the cover, "is for *turisti*. You look like you could use an adventure." She tucked it into the compartment under her seat. "Get on." "I... I really couldn't possibly—" "Get on, or I leave you here to be eaten by the pigeons." She patted the seat behind her. "Your choice, *professore*." He hesitated for a fraction of a second too long. With a sigh of exasperated fondness, she kicked the Vespa back to life. The engine’s growl vibrated through the cobblestones, a direct challenge. *** He got on. His hands hovered uncertainly at her waist as the bike weaved through a maze of narrow alleys, far from the tourist trail. The scent of her—leather, espresso, and something floral, like jasmine—mingled with the exhaust. "You are holding on like I am made of glass!" she shouted over her shoulder, her voice laced with laughter. "Hold on properly, *Inglese*! Or you will be a stain on a Roman wall!" Gingerly, he placed his hands on her jacket. She took a corner sharply, and he instinctively wrapped his arms around her waist, his guidebook forgotten. He could feel the wiry strength in her torso, the confident set of her shoulders. He was a passenger, utterly out of control, and a strange, exhilarating thrill shot through him. *** They stopped at a tiny, crowded café near the Campo de' Fiori. The owner, a burly man with a magnificent mustache, greeted Alessandra like a long-lost daughter, kissing both her cheeks and shouting orders for espresso. "A friend?" Ben asked, slightly breathless. "A complication," she said with a wink. She ordered for them both in a rapid-fire dialect Ben couldn't follow. As they waited, she leaned forward, her elbows on the scarred wooden table. "So, *professore*. What is your great academic passion? The boring bits of history?" "The social impact of urban planning in the early Renaissance, actually," he said, puffing up slightly. Her eyes glazed over with theatrical boredom. "Ah. *Che noia.*" She spotted a tourist at the next table leaving a sleek, expensive-looking pen next to their bill. With a movement so fluid it was almost invisible, her hand swept across the table. The pen vanished into her sleeve. "Tell me," she said, her expression innocent, "did your urban planning include the effect of a beautiful woman on a city's traffic flow?" Ben, who had seen nothing, blinked. "I... beg your pardon?" She just smiled, a secret dancing in her eyes. *** The afternoon was a blur of stolen moments. She dragged him into the cool, hushed interior of a small church, not to pray, but to point out a cherub with a "grumpy face" and whisper a wildly inaccurate history of the saint it depicted. She bought him a gelato from a place with no sign, insisting it was the only real one in Rome. As they sat on the steps of a forgotten piazza, the late afternoon sun painting the ochre buildings gold, Ben found himself laughing, really laughing, for the first time in months. He was dishevelled, his jacket was dusty, and he had no idea where he was. He had never been happier. "You are not what I expected," he said softly, looking at her profile against the ancient stone. She turned to him, her expression unreadable. "And what did you expect, *professore*? A quiet, historical tour?" "Something... safer," he admitted. Alessandra’s smile was a slow, dangerous dawn. She reached out, not for him, but for the small, ornate brass bell hanging from the church door they sat beside. With a deft twist, she unscrewed the tiny clapper and slipped it into her palm. She didn't hide it. She simply held it out to him, a silent offering. He stared at the small piece of metal in her hand, then at her face. The mischief was there, but beneath it, he saw something else—a question, a dare. His heart hammered against his ribs. The polite, rule-following academic in him screamed. But the man who had spent the day on the back of her Vespa, the man who had tasted real gelato and laughed in a dusty piazza, reached out and took the bell. The metal was warm from her touch. "Consider it a souvenir," she whispered, her voice low and intimate in the quiet square. "Of a day outside the guidebook." He closed his fingers around it, the weight of it feeling both trivial and immense. The sun was sinking, and the city was beginning to glow. He had no idea what came next, but for the first time, Ben Carter didn't feel the need to consult a map.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent, engaging day-in-Rome romance with clear character contrast. Alessandra's kleptomania is handled with appropriate subtlety (the pen, the bell clapper), and the bell scene is a well-chosen payoff that ties her secret habit to the emotional climax. Ben's arc—polite academic loosening his grip—is shown through physical detail (hands hovering, then wrapping around her waist; taking the bell) rather than stated outright, which is a strength. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally strains for effect ("her smile was a slow, dangerous dawn," "a mechanical scream"). Some beats are stock—the quirky café owner with the mustache, the "gelato from a place with no sign," the manic pixie energy of Alessandra herself. Her interiority remains thin; she's more a force acting on Ben than a person, though the prompt asks for enigmatic, so this is partly compliant. The Italian phrases are used well. Dialogue is serviceable but sometimes functional rather than sparkling ("A friend?" / "A complication" is a nice touch, though). The ending lands softly and appropriately; the transformation of Ben is small and earned enough. Word count roughly on target. The "" detail was left unfilled, a minor adherence gap. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 72.0
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The hum of the recycler is the only thing keeping the silence from getting too heavy tonight. It’s a slow shift at The Last Outpost, which means I’m polishing the same glass for the third time, just to keep my hands busy. The lighting is low, set to that warm amber that makes everyone look a little less tired and a lot more forgiving of the stains on the upholstery. It’s my favorite time of the cycle, actually. The chaos of the docking rush has faded, leaving just the die-hards and the lonely. I’m halfway through wiping down the mahogany—or whatever synthetic polymer is trying to pass as mahogany this year—when the airlock hisses. He doesn't walk in so much as he falls through the door. He’s tall, or he would be if he wasn't hunched over like he’s trying to hide from the gravity generators. His skin is a shade of pale blue that suggests he’s either been in deep vacuum too long or he’s just naturally unlucky. But it’s the hair that catches the eye. Tentacled dreads, the kind that require high-maintenance bio-gel to keep them from unraveling, and they are currently a mess. One of them is twitching, which usually means high stress or a bad chemical reaction. He stumbles to the bar, bypassing the empty booths, and slides onto the stool right in front of me. He puts his hands on the bar, palms down, and I see the tremble in his fingers. "Vega whisky, neat," he rasps. His voice sounds like gravel in a disposal unit. "Better make that a double." I nod, reaching for the bottle on the top shelf. Vega is expensive, imported from a system that actually has oak trees, not just hydroponic bamboo. "Rough haul?" I ask, pouring the amber liquid. "You have no idea," he mutters. He doesn't look at me. He’s staring at the condensation on the glass like it holds the secrets to the universe. "Usually, when someone comes in looking like they wrestled a squid and lost, it's either a bad trade deal or a woman," I say, sliding the glass over. "Or a squid-woman. We get all types out here on the rim." He lets out a short, sharp laugh that sounds more like a bark. "Just a woman. Sort of." He grabs the glass and downs half of it in one go. He shudders, closing his eyes. "Gods, that burns. Good. I need to feel something other than terror." "Terror is a strong word," I say, leaning my elbows on the bar. "Around here, we prefer 'high-stakes anxiety.' It sounds more professional." He opens his eyes, and for the first time, he really looks at me. His eyes are violet, augmented with tech I don't recognize. "You're Net, right? Nets?" "That's what the sign says," I point to the chalkboard above the register. "And you are?" "Dax," he says. "Dax Vane." The name rings a bell. A distant, dull clanging in the back of my skull. Dax Vane. He’s a runner. A courier for the Syndicate, the loose collective of smugglers who think they run the belt. I’ve seen his face on the bounty boards in the lower decks, but he looks younger in person. More scared. "Okay, Dax," I say, keeping my voice level. "Why are you in my bar? The Syndicate usually drinks at The Rusty Bolt on the other side of the station. They have... looser rules there." "I can't go there," Dax whispers, leaning in closer. The smell of ozone and sweat rolls off him. "I can't go anywhere. I need a ship, Net. I need to get off this rock. Tonight." "Everyone wants a ship, Dax. It's a station. That's sort of the point. But schedules are schedules. The next transport to the core worlds isn't for three days." "I don't have three days!" He slams his hand on the bar, making the glasses jump. His tentacle-dreads flare out in agitation. "I don't have three hours. They're coming." "Who's coming?" I ask, my hand instinctively drifting under the counter where I keep the stun-baton. "The Collector," Dax breathes. The ambient noise of the bar seems to drop a few decibels. In the background, I hear the clatter of a tray, followed by the sharp, distinct shatter of glass hitting the deck plates. Someone dropped a pint. Usually, that would draw a cheer or a groan from the regulars, but the sound just hangs there, brittle and sharp in the sudden quiet. "The Collector," I repeat, keeping my eyes on Dax. "That’s a myth, Dax. A boogeyman the Syndicate bosses use to scare runners into working faster." "He's not a myth," Dax insists, his violet eyes wide and frantic. "I saw him. On Cygnus X-1. I saw what he did to the crew of the *Starlight Maiden*. They weren't just killed, Net. They were... erased. Unraveled. Like they were never there." "Okay," I say, trying to de-escalate. "Let's say I believe you. Why is he after you? Did you lose a package?" "I didn't lose it," Dax says, his voice dropping to a terrified whisper. "I stole it." I stop polishing the glass. "You stole from the Syndicate?" "I stole from *him*," Dax corrects. "The package... it wasn't cargo. It was a key. A genetic key. I was supposed to deliver it to a lab in the nebula, but I got curious. I opened the container." "You never open the container, Dax," I sigh, rubbing my temples. "Rule number one." "I know!" He runs a hand through his twitching dreads. "But I heard it whispering. It was a bio-capsule, Net. Inside was... it was a child. Or something that looked like a child. It had no eyes, just smooth skin, and it was singing." "Singing?" "A frequency. It vibrated in my teeth. It told me things. It told me where it came from. It told me what The Collector does with them." He reaches into his jacket. I tense, ready to duck, but he just pulls out a small, jagged shard of glowing blue crystal. It pulses with a faint, rhythmic light, like a heartbeat. "He's not collecting artifacts," Dax says, staring at the crystal. "He's collecting souls. Or memories. Or whatever you want to call the thing that makes us... us. And he needs more. He's building something, Net. Something big. And he needs this shard to finish it." I look at the crystal. It’s beautiful, in a terrifying, radioactive sort of way. It hums with a low frequency that I can feel in my fillings. "So, you're telling me," I say slowly, "that you have a piece of a soul-stealing super-villain's puzzle in your pocket, and you brought it to my bar?" "I didn't know where else to go!" Dax pleads. "You have a reputation, Net. They say you can get things done. They say you don't ask questions." "I ask questions all the time, Dax. I just don't always listen to the answers." I look around the bar. It’s still quiet. A few patrons are glancing our way, sensing the tension. "Put that away," I hiss. "Now." He shoves the crystal back into his pocket. "I need a ship," he says again, desperation cracking his voice. "I'll pay anything. I have credits. I have uncut spice from the Red Sands. I'll give you the crystal." "I don't want the crystal," I say firmly. "I want you out of here before whoever is looking for you decides to tear my place apart." "I can't leave without a ship," Dax says, his shoulders slumping. "I'm dead if I step out that airlock." I look at him. He’s just a kid, really. In over his head. I’ve seen a hundred like him. They come to the rim to escape something, only to find something worse waiting. Usually, I’d throw him out. Self-preservation is a skill I’ve honed to a razor's edge. But there’s something in his eyes. A genuine, soul-deep terror that I haven't seen in a long time. And that crystal... the hum of it is still in my teeth. "Wait here," I say, turning toward the back room. "Don't move. Don't talk to anyone. And for god's sake, stop twitching." "Where are you going?" he calls after me. "To make a call," I say over my shoulder. "I might know a guy who owes me a favor. But Dax?" "Yeah?" "If this 'Collector' shows up and starts disintegrating my customers, you're paying for the damages." I push through the beaded curtain into the back, the sound of the bar fading behind me. The hum of the crystal seems to follow me, a silent, pulsing warning that I’m stepping into something way over my head. Again.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This chapter executes the prompt's requirements competently. It maintains first-person present tense throughout, keeps a cozy sci-fi register with an undercurrent of menace, establishes a clear conflict (Dax's stolen crystal and the approaching Collector), and leaves that conflict unresolved. Dialogue density comfortably exceeds 60%, and the banter between Nets and Dax carries most of the exposition naturally. Strengths: Nets has a consistent, wry voice ("high-stakes anxiety... sounds more professional"), and the worldbuilding details (Vega whisky from a system with real oak, the chalkboard sign, the Syndicate's preferred bar) are economical and evocative. The dropped pint glass in the sudden quiet is a nice show-don't-tell beat. The pacing is tight, and the ending line ("I'm stepping into something way over my head. Again.") hints at Nets's past without over-explaining. Weaknesses: The plot beats are familiar—the mysterious stranger, the forbidden opened container, the soul-stealing villain, the glowing MacGuffin crystal. "You never open the container, Dax. Rule number one" is a well-worn trope played straight. The Collector as described ("erased... unraveled") is generic menace; the eyeless singing child is evocative but borders on stock creepypasta imagery. Some lines are slightly over-explanatory ("It's beautiful, in a terrifying, radioactive sort of way"), and Dax's terror is mostly stated rather than layered. Nets's decision to help arrives a bit quickly, softened only by a thin gesture at her self-preservation instinct. The prose is clean but rarely rises above functional; there are no truly memorable images beyond the amber lighting and twitching dreads. Overall: a solid, professional genre chapter that hits every instruction but doesn't transcend its tropes. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 59.3
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The saxophone weaves through the humid air, a bluesy wail that feels like it’s coming from the throat of the city itself. It’s noon, but down here, the light is filtered through the wrought-iron lace of the balconies and the neon promises of the bars on Bourbon Street. The heat is a physical weight, sticking my t-shirt to my spine, making the cheap denim of my jeans feel like sandpaper. It’s a Tennessee heat, sure, but thicker. Older. It smells like stale beer, fried dough, and something sweetly rotting that I can’t place. I’m walking, but I don’t know where. My feet are on autopilot, following the river of tourists and locals that flows down the sidewalk. Every person I pass is a potential threat or a potential mark. That’s the new math I’m running in my head. Forty bucks in my pocket. A phone with 11% battery and the location tracking *theoretically* off. A backpack with two changes of clothes and a dog-eared copy of *Orlando* that feels like a pathetic joke right now. “You need to *think*, Taylor,” Mom had said, her voice that brittle, wounded tone that means she’s about to say something unforgivable. I’d thought. I thought for 30 minutes and then I was gone. The sax wails again, and I stop, drawn to the sound like a moth to a flame. It’s coming from a kid, maybe a year or two older than me, sitting on an upturned milk crate outside a souvenir shop selling voodoo dolls and “Fleur-de-lis” shot glasses. He’s Black, with close-cropped hair and eyes that are closed, lost in the music. His sax is dented, loved-looking. I watch his fingers, the way they dance over the keys. It’s easy. It’s the opposite of everything back home, which was all clenched fists and held breaths. “He only plays that one song,” a voice says beside me. I flinch, instinctively pulling my backpack strap tighter. The voice belongs to a girl leaning against the brick wall of the shop. She’s maybe seventeen, with a choppy, dyed-black haircut and a silver ring through her septum. She’s wearing cut-off shorts and a faded band tee I don’t recognize, and she’s smoking a cigarette with the practiced air of someone who’s been doing it for decades. Her eyes, a sharp, cynical blue, are fixed on the musician. “What?” I say, aiming for nonchalance and landing somewhere near ‘strangled’. “The sax,” she says, a plume of smoke punctuating the sentence. “He plays that same mournful riff every day from noon till one. Then he packs up and goes to the soup kitchen for lunch. It’s a whole routine.” She takes a drag, studies me. “You’re not from here.” It’s not a question. I feel my hackles rise, that familiar defensive crouch I learned back home. “How can you tell?” “You look like you’re about to get run over by a horse-drawn carriage,” she says, a ghost of a smirk on her lips. “And you’re staring. Locals don’t stare. We’re all too busy ignoring the magic to notice it.” I don’t know what to say to that. The saxophone player finishes his lament with a long, fading note that hangs in the air like cigarette smoke. He opens his eyes, gives a little nod to a couple who toss change into his open case, and starts packing up. “It’s beautiful,” I blurt out, feeling stupid the second the words are out. “The music.” The girl finally turns her gaze fully on me. It’s intense, like she’s trying to read the fine print on my soul. “Beauty’s a liability down here,” she says, stubbing out her cigarette on the wall. “Means you’ve got something worth taking.” She pushes off the wall, shouldering a backpack that looks improbably small. “You got a place to crash?” The question hits me like a bucket of ice water. *No. No, I don’t. I have forty dollars and a phone I’m afraid to charge.* “I’m… meeting people,” I lie. The words feel like ash in my mouth. She nods, a slow, knowing gesture that makes my stomach clench. “Right. ‘People.’” She starts to walk away, then pauses, looking back over her shoulder. “Name’s CJ.” “Taylor.” I say it before I can think. *Stupid. Why did you say that?* “Well, Taylor,” CJ says, her eyes doing that soul-scan thing again. “If your ‘people’ don’t show, there’s a 24-hour laundromat on Rampart Street. Café Du Monde is open, but the cops’ll roust you if you sleep at a table too long. The real deal is under the overpass by the river. You’ll hear the music from there. Don’t bring anything you don’t want to lose.” She turns and melts into the crowd without another word. I stand there, rooted to the spot, my heart hammering against my ribs. *Under the overpass. Don’t bring anything you don’t want to lose.* She wasn’t talking about my backpack. She was talking about all of it. Hope. Safety. Myself. The crowd flows around me, a river of faces and laughter and shouts. The heat feels even more oppressive now, pressing in from all sides. A profound, crushing loneliness sweeps over me. I am a ghost. No, not a ghost. Ghosts have a history. I’m just a blank space, a question mark in a city full of answers I don’t want to hear. I pull out my phone. 10% battery. I stare at the blank screen, imagining the three missed calls from Mom. The text from my “friend” Jake that just says *dude*. The sheer, pathetic weight of the life I’d tried to run from. But it was *my* life. My boring, suffocating, pre-packaged life. *Be mind-fuckingly bored or invent some drama.* I’d chosen option C: light a match and throw it over my shoulder. CJ’s words echo. *Beauty’s a liability down here.* Is that what I am? A liability? Or just another piece of beauty waiting to be taken? I look back to where the sax player was. The space is empty now, just a scuff mark on the concrete where his crate was. The song is gone, leaving only the random cacophony of the street. I take a deep, shaky breath. The air tastes of opportunity and danger in equal measure. I should find that laundromat. I should charge my phone. I should figure out a plan that extends past the next twenty-four hours. Or I could follow CJ. It’s the stupid choice. The dangerous choice. The choice a kid with a history of “concerning behavioural patterns” would make. But it feels, weirdly, like the first real choice I’ve made since I left home. Not running away. But walking toward something. Even if that something is just a voice in the crowd telling me where the real deal is. I shoulder my backpack, feel the weight of Orlando against my spine, and start walking, merging back into the river. The saxophone is gone, but its ghost is still in my head, a bluesy call to the unknown. And for the first time in 48 hours, the fear in my gut is mixed with something else. A flicker of something like interest.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece adheres well to the prompt: first person, mixed tense, Taylor's voice, internal monologue with conflicting emotions, a mysterious runaway-ish stranger (CJ) with implied secrets, New Orleans atmosphere, roughly the requested length. The prose is competent and evocative, with strong sensory grounding (heat, saxophone, Bourbon Street) and a believable teen voice that echoes the prompt's snark without copying it. The Woolf's *Orlando* detail is a nice character touch. Weaknesses: CJ is a fairly stock figure — the world-weary, chain-smoking street oracle dispensing cryptic wisdom ("Beauty's a liability down here") — and her dialogue occasionally tips into written-to-be-quoted aphorism rather than how a seventeen-year-old actually talks. The saxophone player is pure scenery. The plot is thin: essentially one encounter, some internal spiraling, and a decision to follow CJ. The ending's "flicker of something like interest" is modest and earned, avoiding false uplift, though the "not running away but walking toward something" framing is a touch neat. Some lines edge toward overwrought ("read the fine print on my soul," "a question mark in a city full of answers"). The "new math" of threat-assessment is a good show-don't-tell moment, but the piece also tells emotions directly several times ("A profound, crushing loneliness sweeps over me"). The trans storyline is handled with restraint — present as context rather than melodrama — which is a strength. Overall: solid, professional YA writing with a few clichés and a somewhat static chapter arc. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 72.5
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The morning sun, a pale disc in the perpetually hazy sky, did not so much rise as give up and smear itself across the horizon. Midas sat on an overturned bucket, contemplating the day’s itinerary, which consisted of two items: 1. Don’t die. 2. Find something that wasn’t tinned mystery-meat to eat. Item 1 was a perennial favourite. Item 2 was the ambitious one. Chewy, his companion, sat propped against a pile of salvaged bricks. The animatronic koala’s once-plush fur was now a matted, greyish pelt, and one of his glass eyes had a tendency to drift towards the heavens, as if searching for a long-lost satellite. His internal mechanisms, powered by a solar cell that was more optimistic than functional, emitted a low, constant hum. “Right then, Chewy,” Midas said, addressing the koala with the grave sincerity one reserves for a trusted advisor or a particularly interesting rock. “The larder is bare. The options are: head north to the Old Mall, risk the Scrappers, and maybe find some canned peaches. Or, we go east, into the Whispering Wilds, and forage for… well, for things that haven’t learned to bite back yet.” Chewy’s head tilted with a soft *whirrr-clunk*. His pre-programmed response module, triggered by the word ‘forage,’ kicked in. A tinny, cheerful voice emanated from his chest. “*Remember, kids! A balanced breakfast is the start of a super-duper day!*” “A compelling argument for the Wilds, then,” Midas sighed, hoisting his pack. “Mystery meat it is not. Come on, partner.” Their route took them along a crumbling overpass, where nature was staging a slow, green coup. It was here, scrawled in faded, optimistic blue paint on a concrete pylon, that they found it. **FOLW THE SILENT BIRD TO WHER THE WATER RISES. SAFETY.** Below the words was a crudely painted symbol: a bird in flight, but with no beak. Midas squinted. “The Silent Bird. That’s the old weather vane on the Town Hall, pointing east. And ‘where the water rises’… the old reservoir springs? Chewy, this could be it. A refuge. Maybe even with… *peaches.*” Chewy’s head swivelled towards the graffiti. His good eye focused. “*Fun Fact! Birds are our feathered friends!*” “Precisely.” The mission had a new objective: Follow the cryptic, semi-literate bird to paradise. The first sign of the plan going sideways was literal. The Town Hall weather vane, a proud copper rooster in its former life, was now a headless, silent bird, its directional arrow pointing not east, but straight down into the rubble of the building itself. “Well,” Midas muttered, peering into the dark fissure. “It *is* silent. And it is a bird. Sort of.” The descent was less of a climb and more of a controlled, grunting slide into darkness. They landed in what was once the mayor’s office, now a nest of damp plaster and mutant fungi. It was here they met Gerald. Gerald was a rat. But not just any rat. Gerald was the size of a small terrier, had a single, magnificent horn growing from his forehead, and possessed an air of profound territorial indignation. “Ah,” said Midas, freezing. “A unicorn.” Chewy, whose programming had no subroutine for ‘unicorn,’ defaulted to his social greeting. “*G’day, mate!*” he chirped, his voice echoing in the gloom. Gerald took this as a declaration of war. What followed was not a chase, but a frantic, multi-level negotiation with gravity and architecture. Midas scrambled up a collapsed staircase, Gerald’s horn *thunking* into the wood just behind his heel. Chewy, dropped in the haste, tumbled down a laundry chute, his cheerful voice echoing up from the depths. “*Wheeeee!*” Midas burst out of a fire escape, sprinting without looking, and ran directly into a taut, nearly invisible wire. The world inverted. He found himself dangling by one ankle ten feet in the air, his pack emptying its meagre contents onto the pavement below: a half-eaten bar of something brown, a multi-tool, and a single, miraculously intact tin of peaches. He hung there, swaying gently, watching a one-eyed koala being carried triumphantly on the back of a horned rat down the street below, Chewy’s voice fading into the distance. “*See you later, alligator!*” The return to base was a multi-stage affair. First, there was the slow, humiliating process of sawing through the wire with his own multi-tool while contorted like a pretzel. Then, the trudge back, limping, one sock missing. He arrived to find Chewy already there, sitting neatly by the brick pile, as if he’d taken a taxi. Beside him was a small, perfect pile of acorns. Gerald, apparently, was a host who gave party favours. Midas slumped onto his bucket, the tin of peaches heavy in his hand. He looked at the cryptic message he’d scratched onto a flat piece of slate earlier that morning. He picked up a piece of charcoal and, under the day’s plan, made a single, definitive amendment. **1. Don’t die.** (Status: Achieved, barely.) **2. Find something to eat.** (Status: Achieved, ironically.) **3. Follow the Silent Bird.** (Status: It’s complicated.) He looked at Chewy, whose head was now tilted at a new, jaunty angle, courtesy of his ride with Gerald. The koala’s good eye seemed to stare right at him. “Tomorrow,” Midas said, popping the lid on the peaches with a satisfying *hiss*, “we stay in. And we don’t listen to graffiti.” Chewy’s chest hummed, and a new, never-before-heard phrase crackled out, likely triggered by the jostling. “*Always look both ways before crossing the street!*” Midas ate a peach. It was, against all odds, the most delicious thing he had ever tasted.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a competent, genuinely funny piece that captures Pratchett's wry register reasonably well. The strongest element is Chewy: the animatronic koala whose pre-programmed phrases are comically misaligned with the apocalypse ("A balanced breakfast is the start of a super-duper day!") is a classic Pratchett-style device—the deadpan absurdity of a machine cheerfully narrating catastrophe. The running gag lands repeatedly without wearing thin, and the closing line ("Always look both ways before crossing the street!") is a well-timed final beat. The prose is economical and dry, with good comic timing ("did not so much rise as give up and smear itself across the horizon"). The structure follows the brief faithfully: deliberation, mission going sideways (multiple ways—headless weather vane, Gerald the unicorn rat, the snare), and a return home "worse for wear" in multiple senses (missing sock, dangling upside down, Chewy's new jaunty head tilt). The graffiti plot hook is a nice touch of world-building. Weaknesses: Gerald the horned rat appears abruptly and is resolved a bit too conveniently (the acorn party favours are charming but unearned—why does a territorial rat become a generous host?). The emotional stakes are thin; Midas is a functional comic vehicle rather than a nuanced character, and his relationship with Chewy, while sweet, stays at the level of quips. The "peaches" callback is neat but the ending's "most delicious thing he had ever tasted" is a slightly pat, sentimental close. Some jokes (the numbered list, the status amendments) are effective but border on a familiar post-apocalyptic-comedy formula. The piece is never surprising in its larger shape—competent, but not transcendent. Dialogue is minimal and mostly one-sided (Chewy can't converse), but what exists is well-used. No purple prose, no meandering; the 1000-word target is respected in spirit. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 73.8
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The brass bell above the door of *Celfyddydau Cymreig* jangled violently, more a frantic intrusion than a greeting. A man, all sharp angles in an impeccably tailored coat and dark sunglasses, slammed the door shut behind him and pressed his back against it, breathing hard. Efa looked up from the counter, a half-priced copy of *The Mabinogion* in her hand. "Can I help you, or is the door performing a particular service you require?" The man peeled off his sunglasses, revealing eyes of a startling, cinematic blue. He raked a hand through artfully dishevelled dark hair. "Apologies. Desperate times." "Just the one desperate time, or is this a regular occurrence in Caerphilly?" Efa asked, her tone dry. He offered a smile, the kind that probably launched a thousand merchandise deals. "Rhys Cadwaladr. And you are...?" "Efa. This is my shop. And you're leaning on the non-fiction section's emergency exit." Rhys Cadwaladr. The name clicked into place. Of course. The heartthrob from that gritty Welsh detective series, the one who’d just been cast as a Marvel villain. The paparazzi… "Right. Sorry." He stepped away from the door, his charm-switch flicking on. "Love what you've done with the place. Very... authentic." "It's a bookshop. The books do the heavy lifting," Efa said, not looking up from her re-shelving. "Are you planning on buying one, or just using the ambiance for cover?" "I'll buy ten. Consider it a tax for sanctuary." He wandered, running a finger along a spine. "You have an eclectic taste. A lot of poetry. Dafydd ap Gwilym?" Efa finally met his gaze, a flicker of surprise in her own. "You know ap Gwilym?" "I'm Welsh, not illiterate," he said, his rogueish grin returning. "Played a version of him in a student film years ago. Got a B. The professor said my 'Ode to a Daisy' lacked... 'The Fern's' genuine torment." He shuddered dramatically. "I still have nightmares about the iambic pentameter." "A B?" Efa's lips twitched, the closest she'd come to a smile. "Shocking. I'd have thought you'd be an A-grade seducer of daisies." The door rattled. A camera flash briefly illuminated the dusty windows. Rhys flinched, a real, vulnerable flinch, the charm momentarily dropping. "Could you... is there a back room?" "In the back? Where I keep the valuable first editions and my disappointment? I don't think so." But she saw the genuine panic. The mask had slipped, showing something human and scared underneath. With a sigh, she nodded towards a beaded curtain. "There's a storeroom. Don't knock anything over." He disappeared through the curtain as a reporter's face pressed against the glass. Efa gave the face a flat stare until it moved on. --- In the cramped storeroom, surrounded by cardboard boxes and the smell of old paper, Rhys was pacing. "They're like seagulls with telephoto lenses. You give one a chips and they bring the whole flock." "I wouldn't know. My public is mostly retirees looking for large-print Catherine Cookson novels," Efa said, leaning in the doorway. "You're safe now. They won't come in. I stock nothing of gossip value." "You'd be surprised. 'Rhys Cadwaladr Hiding in Box Fort' has a certain tabloid ring to it." He stopped, looking at her, really looking. "You're not impressed." "Should I be?" "Most people are. It's a reflex. Also, I'm told I'm quite good at my job." "I'm sure you are. But your job is *up there*." She gestured vaguely towards the ceiling, towards the world of screens and premieres. "Down here, you're just a man who can't work a door properly." He let out a laugh, a real one, unforced. "You cut right through it, don't you?" "It saves time." He perched on a box. "Why this? A Welsh-book bookshop in a world of... well, of *that*." He gestured vaguely towards the street. "It's my history. My language. It's real." She paused, her defensiveness softening into something more thoughtful. "When I was ten, my gran's house flooded. Utterly ruined. We lost everything... photo albums, letters, her beloved copy of *Fy Hen Lyfr Plyg*. We were standing in the wreckage, and she just kept saying, 'At least the words are safe. They're in our heads. No water can touch them.' I suppose that stuck with me." Rhys was quiet for a moment. "That's... a hell of a thing to learn at ten." "The world teaches you hard lessons early. Or it does if you're listening." She shrugged. He leaned forward, elbows on his knees. "I did a film once. A World War Two thing. I had to crawl through actual mud, under actual barbed wire, with massive squibs going off around my head. The stunt co-ordinator was a madman. For weeks after, I'd freeze on set if a light popped too loudly. My agent called it 'artistic temperament'. I just called it... fear." He gave a self-deprecating smile. "Not very rogue-like, is it?" "Sounds very human," Efa said softly. The air in the little room changed. The undercurrent was no longer just witty sparring; it was thick with something else, a fragile honesty. "So, the fern," he said, his voice lower. "The genuine torment. What was the professor's note on your work?" Efa blinked. "How did you know I—" "You knew ap Gwilym. You know the fern. You run a bookshop built on words that 'no water can touch'. Spill." She looked away, at a stack of boxes. "I wrote a paper. Called it 'The Necessary Silence Between Words'. About how meaning lives in the pauses, not just the speech. The professor said it was 'technically proficient but emotionally vacant'." "Ouch." "He was right," she said, though her voice was tight. "I was very good at observing the silence. Less good at understanding what was meant to fill it." Rhys stood up. He didn't touch her, but the air between them was charged. "Or maybe," he said, his voice like smoked whiskey, "you were just leaving space. For the right person to come along and make some noise." The moment hung, delicate and terrifying. The beaded curtain rattled. "Rhys? Darling? Are you in there? Your driver's having a fit." A woman, all sleek leather and phone-loaded efficiency, stood glaring. Rhys's entire posture reassembled itself. The charming, slightly hollow public face snapped back on. He turned to Efa, the personal connection vanishing behind a brilliant, generic smile. "Efa. A pleasure. Send me a bill for the ten books." He pulled out a card. "Anything you think I should read to understand... genuine torment." He dropped the card on a box and was gone, swept out by his handler, leaving the scent of expensive cologne and a profound silence. Efa picked up the card. It was simple. Just a name and a number. On the back, in a sharp scrawl, were two words: *Leave space*. She let out a breath she didn't know she'd been holding, her heart hammering against her ribs. The rogue had been disarmed, and in doing so, had completely disarmed her. The silence of the storeroom now felt vast, and achingly, beautifully full of potential noise.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The scene fulfills the brief competently: a famous actor (Rhys Cadwaladr) ducks into a Welsh bookstore, meets the owner (Efa), and their sparring carries the requested undercurrent of chemistry. The dialogue-forward approach is honored, and both voices are distinct — Rhys's performative charm and ego ("I'm told I'm quite good at my job") against Efa's dry deflections. The fragile ego is well realized in his flinch at the camera flash and his need to be liked ("You're not impressed." / "Should I be?"). Efa's inward flusterment is present but somewhat underdeveloped until the final paragraph, where it tips into telling ("had completely disarmed her"). Strengths: the ap Gwilym/poetry exchange is a clever Welsh-specific hook; the gran's flood anecdote is genuinely affecting and earns the "words are safe" motif that pays off in the card's "Leave space"; the handler's interruption is a well-timed beat that snaps Rhys's mask back on, showing rather than telling his public persona. Weaknesses: several stock phrases — "voice like smoked whiskey," "a breath she didn't know she'd been holding," "heart hammering against her ribs" — read as romance-template filler. The ending is slightly over-neat and sentimental ("achingly, beautifully full of potential noise"), and the mutual confession sequence (her paper, his mud-film fear) arrives a touch quickly, making the intimacy feel somewhat accelerated. The "seagulls with telephoto lenses" line is good; "You give one a chips" has a grammatical wobble. Some of the emotional transformation — rogue genuinely disarmed — is asserted rather than fully dramatized. Still, the piece is coherent, well-paced at ~1000 words, and engaging throughout, with only minor clichés and no purple excess. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 74.3
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The heavy iron door groaned open on rusted hinges, the sound echoing down the stone corridor like a dying man’s last breath. Aya stepped through first, her boots barely whispering against the damp flagstones. The underhold air was thick, stale with the scent of mildew and old oil, undercut by something sharper—copper, perhaps, or blood. Gas lamps sputtered in their brackets, casting long, jittering shadows that clung to the walls like living things. *A trap,* she thought, her fingers curling instinctively around the small vial of immateria salts she kept sewn into her glove lining. *The quiet is wrong. The quiet is always wrong.* Katra followed close behind, her hand resting on the flintlock at her hip, eyes scanning the dark. Simeon brought up the rear, his bulk filling the doorway, a cutlass gleaming dully in the lamplight. The three of them moved as one, practiced, silent—until they reached the vaulted chamber at the corridor’s end. And stopped. The chamber was not empty. A dozen figures lined the walls, armed with brass-barreled pistols and short, wicked-looking blades. At the centre of the room, seated upon a crate of smuggled opium as though it were a throne, was a woman Aya had last seen dragged in irons from the guild’s own front gate. Maren Voss. Guildmistress of the Morska. She was not in chains. She was not in a cell. She was here, booted feet crossed at the ankle, a long-barrelled revolver resting across her lap. Her dark hair was pulled back severe and tight, and her coat—black wool, silver buttons—bore no mark of the constabulary. Her smile was thin and sharp as a straight razor. “Ah,” Maren said, her voice low and unhurried, carrying the faint rasp of a lifetime spent breathing harbour smoke. “The prodigals return. I was beginning to think you’d lost your nerve.” Aya’s blood went cold. *She knows. She knew. This was never a raid—it was a cull.* “Guildmistress,” Aya began, keeping her voice level, her accent clipped and aristocratic—a deliberate choice, a mask of its own. “We heard you’d been—” “Arrested?” Maren laughed, a dry, humourless sound. “By whom? The Watch? Those brass-buttoned imbeciles couldn’t find their own arses with a map and a lantern. No, dear girl. I arranged that particular spectacle myself. A test, you might call it. To see which rats would scurry for the cheese.” She gestured lazily, and two of her bodyguards stepped forward—thick-necked men with scarred knuckles and dead eyes. One of them seized Simeon’s arm before he could raise his cutlass. The other drove a fist into his gut, doubling him over with a grunt. Katra reached for her flintlock, but a third guard was faster, slamming the weapon from her hand and twisting her arm behind her back until she cried out. Aya did not run. She did not fight. She stood very still, her heart hammering against her ribs, and met Maren’s gaze. *Think. Think.* “Take the mask,” Maren said. A rough hand seized Aya’s jaw. Another tore the black silk mask from her face. The gaslight caught her features—high cheekbones, pale skin, dark eyes wide with something that was not quite fear. The guards holding her stiffened. Murmurs rippled through the room. “Gods,” one of them breathed. “That’s—she’s—” “Aya Castellan,” Maren finished, rising from her crate with feline grace. She crossed the distance between them in three slow strides, the revolver hanging at her side. “Daughter of Lord Edric Castellan, of the Merchant Council. Granddaughter of the late Alderman Castellan. And—” She paused, leaning close enough that Aya could smell the gun oil on her skin. “—daughter of the witch Elara Castellan, hanged for trafficking in immateria magick. The same magick you’ve been using to claw your way up my guild.” Aya said nothing. Her silence was its own confession. *She knows. She knows everything.* Maren circled her slowly, the way a predator circles wounded prey. “I wondered, you know. How a slip of a girl with soft hands and a finishing-school curtsy managed to summon a shade-wraith in the Thornback warehouse. How she bent the will of Old Niklos without so much as raising her voice. I wondered, and then I had you followed.” She stopped, facing Aya again. “Your mother would be proud. Or horrified. Hard to say which.” “Do what you will with me,” Aya said, her voice steady despite the tremor in her hands. “But Katra and Simeon followed my lead. They’re loyal to the guild. To *you*. They deserve—” “They deserve what all traitors deserve,” Maren cut her off. “A short drop and a sudden stop. As do you.” Silence. The distant harbour foghorn sounded—one, two, three—low and mournful through the stone walls, like the cry of some great dying beast. Aya swallowed. *Stall. Buy time. You are worth more alive than dead.* “You won’t hang me,” she said. Maren raised an eyebrow. “Won’t I?” “You’ll want to,” Aya conceded. “But I’m more valuable to you breathing. I’m a Castellan. My father sits on the Merchant Council. My family controls half the import licences on the eastern docks. If I disappear—if *Aya Castellan* disappears—there will be questions. Investigations. The kind you can’t bribe your way out of.” She paused, letting the words sink in. “But if I’m alive, I’m leverage. A bargaining chip. A key to doors you’ve never been able to open.” Maren studied her for a long moment. Then she smiled, and it was worse than her anger. “Clever girl,” she murmured. “Just like your mother.” She turned away, snapping her fingers. “Chain them. All three. And someone fetch the immateria salts from her glove—carefully, if you please. I’d rather not lose a man to a shade-wraith tonight.” As the guards wrenched her arms behind her back and cold iron bit into her wrists, Aya closed her eyes. *This is not the end,* she told herself. *This is only the beginning of the cost.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response is a competent, professional-grade scene that hits nearly all the prompt's beats: the trio enters the underhold, Maren Voss is revealed free and armed, the trio are captured without a fight scene, Aya is unmasked, and she negotiates her hostage value while internally grappling with exposure. The Victorian/whalepunk texture (gas lamps, flintlocks, brass, harbour fog, opium crates) is well deployed, and the gothic undertone (hanged witch mother, shade-wraiths, dying-beast foghorn) is present without tipping into excess. Strengths: The prose is controlled and atmospheric without drowning in ornamentation. Maren's voice is the standout—rasping, unhurried, predatory, with strong lines ("A short drop and a sudden stop," "Clever girl. Just like your mother"). Aya's internal monologue is economical and functional. The pacing is tight; the ~1000-word target is respected. The reveal that the arrest was staged as a cull is a satisfying twist that reframes the opening. Weaknesses: The plot is conventional—this is a familiar "trap sprung, heroine captured, negotiates" beat, executed well but without much surprise. Katra and Simeon are barely sketched; Simeon exists to be punched, Katra to cry out. The guards' murmured recognition of Aya is a touch convenient. Some phrases edge on stock ("heart hammering against her ribs," "blood went cold," "feline grace"). Aya's negotiation, while logical, resolves almost too easily—Maren capitulates to her logic within a paragraph, which slightly deflates the tension. The ending line ("This is only the beginning of the cost") is a bit pat. The emotional complexity is present but not deep; Aya's dread of exposure is stated more than fully felt. Overall: a polished, engaging genre scene with authentic dialogue and strong atmosphere, held back from excellence by its predictability and thin secondary characters.
