+ Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 75.2
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The morning sun, a colour best described as "apocalyptic beige," filtered through the grimy window of the bus shelter. Midas was engaged in the ancient and noble art of staring at a map, a process which for him invariably involved more hope than cartography. "So," he said, tapping a faded blue line with a dirty finger. "The old Millbrook reservoir. Legend says the pre-Collapse filtration systems were gravity-fed. Meaning, theoretically, we could have clean water without the daily joy of the Pump-Handle Death March." He looked at his companion for confirmation. Chewy, a stuffed koala of indeterminate age, sat propped against a rusted hubcap. One of his ears was permanently bent at a jaunty angle, and his synthetic fur had the texture of a well-loved dishcloth. His only response was a low, whirring hum from somewhere inside his plush torso. "Right. Excellent point," Midas conceded. "The 'theoretically' is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that sentence. But the alternative is another week of drinking boiled puddle water and pretending the green bits are 'flavour.'" Chewy's plastic eyes, which had been a placid, default blue, flickered to a thoughtful shade of amber. It was his 'considering the statistical probability of a horrible death' colour. "I know, I know," Midas sighed, folding the map with the care of a man defusing a bomb made of brittle paper. "But think of it, Chewy. Water that doesn't taste of regret and frog. We go in, we find the intake valve, we check the seals. Simple. In and out." The koala's eyes flashed a bright, optimistic green. It was the 'I believe in you, you magnificent idiot' colour. Midas chose to take it as a good omen. The journey to Millbrook was uneventful, which in the post-Collapse world was the most alarming event of all. They navigated the skeletal remains of a motorway, where cars sat in silent, rusting queues, their occupants long since departed for appointments they would never keep. Midas carried Chewy in a modified hiking pack, the koala's head poking out like a furry periscope. They found the reservoir, a concrete behemoth squatting in a valley of overgrown weeds. The main gate was, of course, welded shut. This was a problem. Midas, however, possessed a problem-solving toolkit that consisted primarily of optimism and a crowbar. "There's a drainage pipe," he announced, pointing to a dark, ominous hole near the base of the dam. "It's probably just a bit… sludgy." Chewy's eyes turned a deep, doubtful purple. The pipe was more than sludgy. It was a subterranean ecosystem of its own. Midas slid in with a squelch and a curse, the sound echoing in the darkness. He landed in something that was less 'water' and more 'sentient mud.' Chewy, strapped to his back, let out a series of concerned, high-pitched whirs. "Almost there," Midas grunted, wading through the muck. "Just a bit further." This was, of course, the exact moment the floor gave way. They didn't fall far, but they landed with a definitive *splash* into a chamber filled with what smelled suspiciously like fermented history. The pipe they'd come through groaned ominously, and a cascade of rust and concrete sealed their exit. "Well," Midas said, spitting out a mouthful of unidentifiable sludge. "That's suboptimal." Chewy's eyes were a furious, flashing red. It was his 'I am experiencing the emotion you humans call "I told you so"' colour. Their new prison was the main filtration chamber. It was vast, dark, and, most importantly, completely devoid of the 'clean water' they had sought. Instead, it was full of the same primordial ooze they were standing in. The legendary gravity-fed system had, it seemed, long since succumbed to the gentle persuasion of gravity and entropy. "Okay, new plan," Midas announced to the echoing darkness. "We find another way out." This involved climbing. Midas, whose relationship with vertical surfaces was best described as 'acrimonious,' found a rusted maintenance ladder. He began to ascend, his boots slipping on the corroded rungs. Chewy, still on his back, offered no encouragement, his eyes a steady, unimpressed grey. Halfway up, a rung gave way. Midas yelped, dangling by one hand. The pack shifted, and Chewy, with the slow, inevitable grace of a falling dream, slid out and plunged back into the ooze below with a sad, wet *plop*. "Chewy!" Midas yelled, his voice cracking. He scrambled back down, slipping and sliding until he was waist-deep in the muck again. He fished around frantically until his hand closed on a familiar, sodden shape. He pulled the koala out. Chewy was dripping, his fur matted, his jaunty ear now drooping with despair. His eyes were dark, the colour of a dead screen. Midas held him close. "I'm sorry, buddy. I'm so sorry." For a long moment, there was only the sound of dripping water. Then, one of Chewy's eyes flickered. It was a faint, weak light, but it was there. A pale, forgiving blue. They sat in the dark for what felt like hours, the only light coming from Chewy's single, steadfast eye. It was Midas who finally noticed it. A faint breeze, carrying the scent of dust and freedom, was coming from a crack in the far wall. It led to a series of old ventilation shafts. The escape was a miserable, claustrophobic crawl through tight, metal tunnels. Midas went first, dragging the damp Chewy behind him. They emerged, blinking, into the late afternoon sun, on the opposite side of the dam from where they'd entered. They were covered head to toe in filth, smelling like a forgotten corner of a swamp god's basement, and were carrying zero litres of clean water. They trudged back towards their bus shelter, a pair of mud-encrusted spectres of failure. Midas didn't speak. He just clutched his koala, who was slowly drying in the breeze, his fur starting to fluff up again. Back at the shelter, Midas gently cleaned Chewy with a relatively clean rag, wiping the gunk from his plastic eyes. He set the koala down and looked at him. "So," Midas said, his voice raspy. "The reservoir was a bust." Chewy's eyes glowed a steady, unwavering blue. It wasn't green, or amber, or red. It was just… blue. A calm, steady 'we are alive, and that is enough' blue. Midas managed a small, tired smile. "Yeah," he said, slumping down beside his friend. "You're right. Tomorrow, we'll just go back to the Pump-Handle Death March. At least we know how that one ends." He leaned his head back against the bus shelter wall, and for the first time all day, felt the distinct possibility of a future, however grubby. Chewy's eyes glowed softly in the growing twilight, a tiny, mechanical beacon in the ruins of the world.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent, wry post-apocalyptic adventure that hits the requested beats: deliberation at home base, a mission that goes sideways in escalating stages, and a return home worse for wear. The Pratchett influence shows in the dry asides ("apocalyptic beige," "the 'theoretically' is doing a lot of heavy lifting") and the affectionate mockery of the protagonist's optimism, though it never quite reaches Pratchett's footnoted digressiveness or true comic density — the humor is more gently amusing than laugh-out-loud. Chewy is the story's best invention: an animatronic koala who communicates only through eye-color changes, which Midas translates. This is a clever solution to the "one character can't talk" problem, and the running gag of naming each color ("the 'I told you so' colour") is charming. However, the device becomes slightly mechanical through repetition, and Chewy's near-death flicker-and-recovery is a small emotional beat that resolves a touch too easily. Midas is consistent — hapless, hopeful, prone to understatement — and his actions (crowbar optimism, acrimonious relationship with ladders) are believable within the genre. The prose is clean and flows well, with good sentence rhythm and some genuinely nice images ("a furry periscope," "appointments they would never keep"). The mud-chamber sequence is vividly unpleasant in a good way. Weaknesses: the plot is predictable in its broad strokes (mission fails, escape, trudge home), and the ending's gentle uplift — "we are alive, and that is enough" — is earned but borders on sentimental, slightly at odds with the wry tone. Dialogue is one-sided by design, which limits its range, though Midas's half of it is well-handled. Nothing is purple or overwrought; the piece shows restraint. It's a solid, professional, likeable story that lacks the spark of a masterpiece. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 76.3
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The rain was coming down in sheets, blurring the lights of The Hayes into watercolour streaks. Inside, *Y Storiwr* – The Storyteller – was quiet, smelling of old paper, lemon polish, and brewing tea. Efa was shelving a new consignment of poetry, humming along to the low thrum of the Welsh-language radio, when the door flew open with a jangle of bells and a gust of damp air. A man stumbled in, pulling the door shut behind him with a thud. He was tall, dressed in a ridiculously expensive-looking leather jacket now dark with rain, and he was breathing as if he’d just run a marathon. He leaned against the door, eyes wide, staring out through the glass. Efa put down her book. “We’re closing in ten minutes.” The man didn’t seem to hear. He flinched as a flash went off outside, then ducked his head, turning away from the window. “Right. Of course. Sorry.” His voice was a low, smooth baritone, laced with an accent that was pure, polished London. He ran a hand through his dark, rain-slicked hair, pushing it back from a face that was, Efa had to admit, unfairly handsome. All sharp cheekbones and a jaw that could cut glass. He looked vaguely, irritatingly familiar. “You can’t just stand by the door,” she said, her tone flat. “You’re letting the damp in.” He turned, and the full force of his attention landed on her. A slow, devastating smile spread across his face. It was a weaponised smile, the kind she’d seen on billboards. “Of course. My apologies. I’m just… escaping the hounds.” He gestured vaguely towards the street. “Do you get many of those around here? Paparazzi?” “Only when someone like you decides to grace us with their presence,” Efa said, turning back to her poetry shelf. “The coffee shop next door is more their speed. Better lighting for a candid shot.” He laughed, a rich, practiced sound. “You’re not wrong.” He took a few steps deeper into the shop, his expensive boots silent on the worn wooden floor. He looked around, his eyes scanning the towering shelves, the little reading nooks, the cat sleeping on a pile of maps. “This is a proper place. A sanctuary. I’m Rhys, by the way.” He said his name like it was a gift. Efa paused, a slim volume of R.S. Thomas in her hand. Rhys Llewelyn. Of course. The man who’d just won a BAFTA for playing a tortured Welsh poet. The irony was not lost on her. “I know who you are,” she said, not turning around. “I’m the woman who is trying to close her shop.” “Right. The closing woman. A noble profession.” He leaned against a shelf labelled ‘Hanes’ – History. “And you are…?” “Busy.” His smile faltered for a fraction of a second, a flicker of surprise in his eyes. He wasn’t used to this. He recovered instantly, the charm dialling back up. “A woman of mystery. I like it. You run this whole place yourself?” Efa finally turned to face him fully. He was watching her, his head tilted, a genuine curiosity now warring with the performance. “It’s my shop. So yes.” “It’s wonderful,” he said, and for a moment, it sounded like he meant it. “It feels… real. Not like those curated, minimalist places in London that smell of nothing.” He took a step closer, picking up a book from a nearby table. He ran a thumb over the worn cover. “So, what’s the story of this place, then? *Y Storiwr*.” “It’s a bookstore,” Efa said, her voice dry. “People buy books. They read them. Some of them even bring them back.” He laughed again, but this time it was softer, less performative. “You’re a tough crowd. Most people, when they meet me, they want an autograph. A selfie. They tell me their life story.” “Most people aren’t trying to cash up a register and get home before the last bus.” “Ah, but I’m not most people,” he said, the roguish glint returning to his eye. He was back on script. “I’m Rhys Llewelyn. I could make this little shop famous. A post on my Instagram… ‘Found this hidden gem in Cardiff, a real-life Diagon Alley run by a sharp-tongued enchantress.’ You’d have queues down the street.” Efa felt a prickle of irritation, and beneath it, something else. A flicker of heat. He was so close now she could smell his cologne, something expensive and woody that cut through the scent of old books. She refused to be another adoring fan. “I don’t need queues down the street,” she said, meeting his gaze directly. “I need to pay my rent. And I’m not an enchantress. I’m just Welsh. We don’t suffer fools gladly.” The barb hit. She saw it in the slight tightening of his jaw, the way his smile became a little brittle. His need for approval was a palpable thing, a low hum beneath the surface of his charm. Her refusal to provide it was, she realised with a jolt, more interesting to him than any fawning praise. “Fools?” he asked, his voice quieter. “Is that what I am?” “You’re a man hiding from cameras in a bookshop on a Tuesday night,” Efa said, softening her tone just a little. “I’d call that foolish, wouldn’t you?” He stared at her, the actor’s mask slipping. For a second, she saw the man underneath: tired, a little lost, and strangely vulnerable. The silence stretched, filled only by the drumming of the rain and the faint Welsh lilt from the radio. The chemistry, previously a sparring match, now hummed with a different, more potent frequency. “Perhaps,” he conceded, his voice barely a whisper. He put the book down. “So, what do you recommend? For a fool.” Efa’s heart was thumping against her ribs. She felt flustered, exposed, but she held his gaze. She walked over to the poetry section, her fingers tracing the spines. She pulled out a slim, modern collection. “Try this,” she said, holding it out to him. “It’s about finding beauty in small, ordinary things. It might be a useful perspective.” He took the book, his fingers brushing against hers. A spark, clean and sharp as static electricity, jumped between them. They both pulled back slightly. “*Ordinary Things*,” he read the title aloud. He looked from the book to her, a slow, genuine smile finally reaching his eyes. It wasn’t his camera smile. It was smaller, more uncertain, and infinitely more charming. “Right,” Efa said, her voice a little unsteady. She took a step back, putting some much-needed distance between them. “That’ll be eight pounds fifty. And we’re definitely closed now.” He fumbled in his jacket, pulling out a wallet. As he handed over a ten-pound note, his eyes met hers again. “Thank you,” he said, and he wasn’t talking about the book. “Don’t mention it,” Efa said, her fingers closing around the crisp note. “And Mr. Llewelyn?” “Rhys,” he corrected softly. “The back exit leads to St. Mary Street. The paparazzi never look there.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The scene fulfills the brief competently: a famous actor (Rhys Llewelyn) ducks into a Welsh bookstore, spars with the owner (Efa), and the dynamic of charm-offensive vs. immunity plays out with the requested undercurrent of mutual attraction. The Welsh setting is well-textured (Welsh-language radio, "Y Storiwr," R.S. Thomas, St. Mary Street), and the dialogue carries most of the scene as instructed. Rhys's fragile ego is shown through his faltering smile and need for approval; Efa's flustered interior is conveyed through her heartbeat and unsteady voice, though some of this is told rather than shown ("She refused to be another adoring fan," "The chemistry... now hummed with a different, more potent frequency"). The prose is clean and controlled, with a few nice images (watercolour streaks, the "weaponised smile"), though occasionally it leans on familiar romance tropes—the static-electricity touch, the "he wasn't talking about the book" line, the jaw that could cut glass. The ending is neat and satisfying, if slightly predictable. The voices are distinct: Rhys performs, Efa deflects dryly. Some beats are a touch on-the-nose (narrator explicitly explaining what his need for approval means to him), and the emotional turn happens a bit quickly, but it's earned within a single scene. Overall a solid, professional piece of commercial romance writing—engaging, coherent, and well-paced, without reaching genuine brilliance or originality. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 80.5
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Morska Conspiracy — Chapter IV: The Underhold The door groaned on its hinges like a whale dying in shallows. Aya had expected resistance — wards, perhaps, or the brittle *crack* of a tripmine left by careless hands in the chaos of the morning's raid. She had not expected silence. The underhold breathed it back at her: damp, mineral, ancient. The gas lamps that lined the corridor had been turned low, their mantles guttering in uneven rhythm, as though the very walls were drawing shallow breaths. "This isn't right," Katra murmured at her shoulder. "No," Aya agreed. "It isn't." Simeon said nothing. He rarely did. He simply checked the oil on the mechanism of his hand-cannon with a click that echoed far too loudly in the stairwell, and nodded once. *Forward.* They descended. The underhold of the Morska Guild had been carved from the old whaling docks — not the dockyards themselves, but the catacombs beneath, where generations of merchants had stored oil and bone and ambergris in the days before the Scythan trade made such things quaint. The walls sweated brine. Fossilized vertebrae jutted from the stone at intervals, enormous and pale, like the ribs of some cathedral built by a god with a fisherman's sense of humour. Aya kept her hand near the seam of her coat where she kept the focus-stone — a shard of immateria-saturated obsidian she'd stolen from her mother's estate three years before the constabulary came for her. Before the rope. She did not allow herself to think of the rope. Not now. They reached the antechamber. The great vault door — eighteen inches of cast whalebone and riveted steel — stood open. Not broken. *Open.* "I see," Aya breathed. The antechamber beyond was wide and low-ceilinged, its far wall dominated by the reliquary alcove where the Scythan artifact was meant to rest behind a locked gate of cold iron. The alcove was empty. The cold iron gate hung open like a mouth mid-scream. And seated before it, in a high-backed chair of blackened oak that had no earthly business being this deep underground, was Commander Vessra Lockwell. She did not look arrested. She looked *amused.* Vessra Lockwell was a tall woman, lean as a harpoon, with steel-grey hair pulled back so tightly it seemed to pull her sharp features into a permanent expression of quiet appraisal. She wore her whalebone-stitched longcoat — the one the constables supposedly found splattered with evidence of the Dock Street killings — clean and pressed. In her left hand, she held a glass of something amber. In her right, resting across her knee, she held a short-barrelled rook gun, its brass cylinder catching the gaslight. Six figures stood in the shadows behind her. Guild muscle. Not the panicked, scattered remnants Aya had expected. Disciplined. Armed. Waiting. "Oh, *do* come in," Vessra said, as though she were hosting afternoon tea and not an ambush. "I've been waiting rather patiently." Aya's blood turned to ice water. Every calculation, every contingency she and Katra and Simeon had mapped over the preceding hours — all of it wrong. Not merely wrong. *Designed* to be wrong. *She let herself be taken. She orchestrated the raid. She—* "Tendra," Vessra called, without looking away from Aya. "The mask." One of the figures moved. He was quick, built like a dockland bruiser, and he reached Aya before she could summon so much as a whisper of the immateria. Hands like ship's tackle seized her wrists. Another hand found the black silk mask she wore — a theatre piece, half-comedy, half-necessity — and tore it from her face. The cold air hit her cheeks like a slap. "Ah," Vessra said, and something shifted in her expression. Not surprise, exactly. Recognition. "Lady Aya Voss-Carrenthian. I did wonder." "Don't—" Katra started, reaching for the blade at her hip, but two more figures materialized from the shadows, and the unmistakable *chk-chk* of a loaded oil-rifle silenced her. Simeon, for his part, raised his hands slowly. His hand-cannon clattered to the stone floor. He looked at Aya, and in his dark eyes she read what she already knew: *It's over.* Vessra rose from her chair. She was taller standing. She always had been. Aya had seen her once, years ago, at a function her father had dragged her to — some port authority gala heavy with pipe smoke and lies. Vessra had been a guest of honour then. A civic pillar. The woman who kept the docks *civilized.* "Bind them," Vessra said. "Gently. She's worth more unbruised." Rough hemp bit into Aya's wrists behind her back. She was shoved to her knees. The stone was wet and merciless beneath her. *Think. Think, you foolish girl.* "You've made an error, Commander," Aya said, and was distantly proud that her voice did not crack. "Have I?" "The constabulary raid. The arrest. It was theatre, clearly — you arranged it yourself, or let it happen, to flush out dissent. But you need me alive and *coherent* for whatever leverage I represent, and that gives me time you don't intend to grant." Vessra stopped. She tilted her head, the way a shark might tilt before deciding whether to bite. "Time," Vessra repeated. "You want *time.*" "I am the daughter of House Voss-Carrenthian. My father sits on the Harbour Commission. My disappearance — my *death* — would bring the Admiralty's fingers into your little operation within a day. You don't want the Admiralty's fingers. No one does." "And your father knows about your nocturnal activities, does he?" *No.* The word landed in Aya's chest like a harpoon. "He doesn't need to," she said. "He will tear this city apart regardless." "She's right," Katra said from the floor, where two guards held her face-down. "Kill her and you've bought yourself a war you can't win." Vessra looked at Katra for a long moment, then returned her gaze to Aya. She crouched, bringing their eyes level. Up close, her face was a map of years — scars, sun-damage, the grey pallor of a woman who'd spent her life beneath the gas lamps of port cities. She smelled of gun oil and something older. Something maritime. "Your mother," Vessra said quietly, "could summon things from the dark between the walls of the world. They hanged her for it." She paused. "You can do the same, can't you?" Aya said nothing. "I've known for some time," Vessra continued, rising. "Why do you think I allowed you to climb so high, so quickly? A girl with *that* gift, in *my* guild?" She smiled, and it did not reach her eyes. "You are not a hostage, Lady Aya. You are an *asset.* And assets are so much more useful when they understand they have no alternative." The gas lamps flickered. Somewhere deep in the underhold, water dripped in a slow, metronomic rhythm — like a clock counting down to something Aya could not yet name. She swallowed. *The rope,* she thought. *Always the rope, waiting at the end.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response is a strong execution of the prompt. It hits all required story beats: the trio enters the underhold, finds Vessra un-incarcerated with bodyguards, Aya is unmasked, all three are captured without a fight scene, and Aya attempts hostage-negotiation while internally grappling with exposure of her aristocratic identity and her mother's fate. The twist that Vessra orchestrated her own arrest and has long known about Aya's gift is a satisfying escalation that deepens the trap rather than resolving it. The whalepunk/Victorian aesthetic is well-realized: whalebone vault doors, catacombs beneath whaling docks, ambergris, gas lamps, brass cylinders, oil-rifles, "men trust brass and oil and steel" is embodied rather than stated. Gothic horror elements (the empty reliquary "like a mouth mid-scream," the dripping metronome, the recurring rope imagery) are effective. Dialogue is period-appropriate and distinct — Vessra's urbane menace ("Oh, do come in") contrasts nicely with Katra's blunter interjections and Simeon's near-silence. Aya's internal monologue is well-integrated and thematically consistent (the rope, her mother, self-recrimination). Weaknesses: some phrases strain slightly ("like a whale dying in shallows" is an odd simile to open with; "a god with a fisherman's sense of humour" is cute but borders on precious). The reveal that Vessra knew all along is a familiar trope, executed competently but not freshly. A few beats are telegraphed (the empty alcove, the "designed to be wrong" realization). Simeon remains undercharacterized, though that's arguably intentional. The prose occasionally leans ornate but stays this side of purple. The ending is appropriately ominous and earned — the "asset not hostage" reversal gives the darkness weight rather than cheap shock. Overall this is polished, coherent, engaging genre fiction that fulfills nearly every instruction with craft. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 74.1
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gunpowder Rendezvous The ceiling fan rotates like a tired propeller, stirring nothing. Smoke clings to the low beams of the El Rey Cantina like a second ceiling, thick and yellow and permanent. The bartender—a bald man with a scar bisecting his left eyebrow—hasn't looked up in twenty minutes. He doesn't need to. He already knows what everyone in his bar is worth. Spike Spiegel sits at the far end of the bar, his long legs stretched out beneath him, one heel hooked on the crossbar of his stool. A glass of beer sweats in front of him, mostly ignored. His cigarette, however, is not ignored. It burns between his fingers like a tiny, faithful companion, and he exhales a stream of smoke toward the ceiling fan with the particular laziness of a man who has decided that gravity can do most of the work for him. He's been waiting for forty minutes. The bounty board said 9:00 PM. The contact said the back booth. The job—a two-million-woolong grab on a rogue arms dealer named Kessler—paid well enough to keep the Bebop flying for a month. Enough to keep Faye quiet. Enough to keep Ed in instant noodles. The door opens. She doesn't walk in so much as detonate into the room. Short black crop top, shorts that leave nothing to imagination or modesty, and two Custom M1911s sitting in thigh holsters like sleeping pit bulls. Her dark hair spills over one shoulder, and her eyes—sharp, dark, furious—sweep the bar with the practiced efficiency of someone who has already identified every exit, every weapon, and every threat. Spike watches her in the mirror behind the bar. He doesn't turn around. His reflection watches her for him. She spots the back booth. It's empty. She spots the bartender. She spots Spike. She walks toward him. Her boots strike the floor with deliberate weight—each step a statement, each step a countdown. "You Spike?" she says. "Depends who's asking," he says. He still doesn't turn around. "I'm the person who's going to put a bullet in your kneecap if you don't answer the question." He finally turns, leaning on his stool, and looks at her with his mismatched eyes. His left eye—the real one—is half-lidded, amused. His right eye—the prosthetic, the dead one—stares through her without blinking. "Spike Spiegel," he says. "And you're Revy." She slides into the booth and kicks her legs up onto the table, crossing her ankles. The motion draws his eye despite himself, and he sees her notice him noticing. She grins—a blade wrapped in lip gloss. "So we're both here for Kessler," she says. "Funny." "Funny," he agrees. "You want a drink?" "I want the bounty." "Wanting and having are two different things." She snorts. He orders her a bourbon, neat, without asking. She takes it when it arrives and drinks half of it in one pull. The bartender watches this with the blank expression of a man who has seen women drink men under tables. He has. This one could. "So what's your play?" Spike asks. "My play is I walk in, I shoot Kessler, and I walk out with the bounty. Simple." "You make it sound easy." "Everything's easy when you're better than everyone else in the room." He smiles at that—not a grin, not a smirk, but a real smile, thin and crooked, the kind that surfaces only when something surprises him. She surprises him. He lights another cigarette and offers her one. She takes it without hesitation, leaning in so he can light it. Their faces are close. He can smell gunpowder and cheap whiskey and something underneath both—something warm, something human. "You're not bad-looking," she says, exhaling smoke past his ear. "For a dead man." He blinks. "What makes you say I'm a dead man?" "Your eyes. Both of them. One looks like it's seen too much, and the other one doesn't look like it's seen anything at all." Something shifts behind his face—a crack in the plaster, quickly sealed. He leans back and shrugs. "Whatever happens, happens," he says. --- It happens at midnight. They find Kessler at a warehouse on the docks, flanked by four armed guards and a wall of crates filled with stolen military hardware. Revy wants to go in shooting. Spike wants to go in quiet. They argue about it in whispers behind a rusted shipping container, their shoulders almost touching. "Quiet means I get the bounty," he says. "Shooting means I get the bounty faster." "Faster isn't always better." "Spoken like a man who's never had anything worth rushing toward." That lands. He looks at her. She looks at him. The warehouse hums with fluorescent light and distant machinery. They compromise. Revy goes loud. Spike goes quiet. Kessler goes down between them—Revy's bullet taking his left shoulder, Spike's fist taking his jaw, and then they're standing over him, both breathing hard, both reaching for him at the same time. Their hands touch on his collar. Neither pulls away. "My bounty," she says. "Half," he says. "The whole thing." "Half, or we both lose it to the next guy who shows up." She stares at him. Then she smiles, and it's different this time—not a blade, but something sharper. A crack. "Half," she says. --- The motel room is twelve dollars a night and worth every penny of that. They check in under false names—his is "Jett," hers is "Rebecca"—and the clerk doesn't ask questions. Motels on the edge of cities don't ask questions. That's the business model. She sits on the bed and begins cleaning her guns with ritual precision. He leans against the wall near the window and smokes. The bounty transfer is processing. In three hours, the money splits and they go their separate ways. The silence between them is a loaded weapon. "You're not what I expected," she says. "What did you expect?" "Someone who talks less." "You're not what I expected either." "Good or bad?" He doesn't answer. She stands and walks toward him, stopping close—closer than the warehouse, closer than the bar. She can feel the heat from his cigarette between them. He can see the dragon tattoo rippling along her arm as she lifts it and takes the cigarette from his fingers, drags from it, hands it back. "Your hands are steady," she says. "So are yours." "Not for long." She kisses him—or he kisses her—or it happens somewhere in the no-man's-land between them, and it tastes like bourbon and gunpowder and cigarettes, and it lasts exactly as long as it should before they both pull back, breathing hard. "You're trouble," he says. "Look in the mirror, dead man." He laughs—a real laugh, brief and broken and beautiful—and she watches it happen like she's watching something she doesn't have a word for. Outside, a siren wails somewhere. The ceiling fan in the lobby spins on. Neither of them moves to leave. Whatever happens, happens.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers a competent, atmospheric crossover that hits all the requested beats: seedy bar, drinking, competitive banter, gunplay against Kessler, and a motel room standoff that resolves into mutual tension rather than resolution. The prose is tight and controlled, with some genuinely strong images—"She doesn't walk in so much as detonate into the room," "The silence between them is a loaded weapon," "a blade wrapped in lip gloss." The mirrored structure (bar → warehouse → motel) gives the piece a clean escalation arc. Character work is largely faithful. Spike's fatalism, prosthetic eye, and "Whatever happens, happens" mantra are woven in naturally, and Revy's aggression, chain-smoking, and vulnerability-through-cracks are well captured. The observation about his two eyes—"One looks like it's seen too much, and the other one doesn't look like it's seen anything at all"—is the strongest line in the piece and a smart use of his canonical detail. Weaknesses: the dialogue, while serviceable, leans on hardboiled clichés ("Wanting and having are two different things," "You're trouble"). The warehouse gunplay is compressed to the point of feeling like a summary rather than a scene—the action the prompt requested is dispatched in a single paragraph. The motel standoff resolves a bit too smoothly; the "or he kisses her—or it happens somewhere in the no-man's-land between them" construction is elegant but slightly evasive, dodging the standoff's full tension. The ending's repetition of Spike's mantra is a nice bookend but borders on pat. Revy's vulnerability surfaces mostly through narrated assertion rather than dramatized moment. The bartender's "He has. This one could" fragment is a nice touch, but the piece occasionally tells us things ("She surprises him") rather than letting us feel them. Still, the voice is consistent, present tense is maintained throughout, the tone stays noir without tipping into parody, and the piece is coherent and economical. It's a solid, professional piece of fan fiction that doesn't quite transcend its genre trappings. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 56.3
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The mist was the first thing I remember about that night. It clung to the edges of the burial mound like a living thing, glowing a sickly, bone-white under the moon. Astrid called it *myrk*, the old word for darkness and fog. To me, it just looked like a warning. We’d been in Norrbotten for six months. Six months of my father’s forced cheerfulness, my mother’s quiet sighs, and the crushing, endless silence of the pines. Stockholm felt like a dream I’d had about someone else’s life. Then I met Astrid. She was all sharp angles and sharper smiles, with a confidence that felt ancient. Her grandmother, she claimed, was a *klok kvinna*—a wise woman—and had taught her things. Not just folk tales, but *practices*. Astrid called them “midnight games.” We’d whisper a name over a candle flame to learn their secrets, or bury a lock of hair to make a boy notice you. It felt thrilling, transgressive, a secret language against the backdrop of my beige new life. Útiseta, she’d explained, was the ultimate game. “Sitting out,” she’d said, her eyes gleaming in the dim light of her attic room. “On a place of the old dead. At the turn of the night. You sit, and you don’t move, and you don’t speak. And you listen. The mound… it remembers. It’ll give you knowledge. Real knowledge.” I’d agreed, of course. What else was there to do? Now, standing at its base, the mound seemed less like a game and more like a challenge. It was a low, grassy hump in the middle of a field, ringed by ancient, leaning stones. The air was cold, the kind that seeps into your bones. “Remember the rules,” Astrid whispered, her breath a white plume. “No talking. No looking back once you’re seated. And whatever you hear, whatever you feel… you don’t break the circle.” She handed me a small, smooth stone from the river. “For grounding. In case it gets too much.” Her tone was matter-of-fact, as if she were giving me a shopping list. She produced a small, folded cloth from her pocket. Inside were three items: a rusted iron nail, a dried sprig of juniper, and a lock of blonde hair. I recognized the hair. It was from Elsa, the girl who’d made a snide comment about my city clothes last week. “What’s that for?” I asked, my voice thin. “A focus,” Astrid said, not meeting my eye. “To direct the… listening. Don’t worry about it. Just part of the ritual.” She placed the items in a small, hollow depression at the mound’s peak. Then she took my hand. Her palm was dry and calloused. “Ready?” I wasn’t. But I nodded. We climbed. The grass was damp, slick under my sneakers. The mist swirled around our ankles, then our knees, as if the mound were swallowing us. At the top, the world shrank to a circle of about ten feet, bounded by the fog. The moon was a hazy disc above. “Sit,” Astrid commanded, pointing to two flat stones she’d placed earlier. They were cold through my jeans. She sat on the other, pulling her knees to her chest. “Now. Silence.” The first few minutes were just… cold. My teeth chattered. I focused on the stone in my hand, its smooth weight. I listened to the wind in the distant pines, the frantic beat of my own heart. This is stupid, I thought. We’re just two kids sitting on a hill. Then the sounds began. It started as a low hum, so deep I felt it in my sternum before I heard it with my ears. I glanced at Astrid. Her eyes were closed, her face serene. The hum grew, resolving into something like a voice, but not. It was the sound of many whispers layered over each other, a static of sibilance and breath. I couldn’t make out words, but the *intent* was clear. It was curious. It was circling. I squeezed the river stone. *It’s the wind. It’s the blood rushing in my ears. It’s the power of suggestion.* The whispers sharpened. One voice, clearer than the rest, seemed to peel away from the chorus. It was a woman’s voice, thin and reedy. It said a name. *Elsa.* My blood ran cold. It was the name from the lock of hair. Astrid’s eyes snapped open. She didn’t look at me, but a small, satisfied smile touched her lips. She’d heard it too. The whispers changed, became a chorus of that one name, chanting it. *Elsa. Elsa. Elsa.* It wasn’t a threat, not exactly. It was an acknowledgment. A focusing. I felt a sudden, visceral image in my mind: Elsa, crying in the school hallway, her face blotchy. The image was so sharp, so real, it was like a memory that wasn’t mine. I wanted to scream. I wanted to run. But the rules. *Whatever you hear, you don’t break the circle.* The chanting stopped. The silence that followed was worse. It was a heavy, listening silence. Then, I felt it. A pressure. Not on my body, but on my *mind*. It was like someone pressing a thumb against the inside of my skull, testing the walls. It was searching. It was hungry. Astrid let out a soft, shaky breath. “It’s here,” she whispered, breaking her own rule. Her voice was filled with a terrifying awe. The pressure increased. I saw flashes: my father’s tired face, my mother’s lonely eyes, a memory of my old bedroom in Stockholm, the smell of rain on hot pavement. It was rifling through me, pulling out my own secrets, my own sadness, to make a space for itself. This wasn’t knowledge from beyond. This was an exchange. It was taking. The mist at the edge of the mound began to coalesce. It thickened, pulling inward, forming shapes that were almost human but not quite—elongated limbs, hollows where faces should be. They weren’t coming for me. They were coming for the offering. For Elsa. “Don’t look,” Astrid hissed, her own fear finally breaking through. She grabbed my arm, her nails digging in. “Linnea, don’t look at them!” But I couldn’t help it. I turned my head, just a fraction. In the swirling fog, for one heartbeat, I saw a face. It was pale and gaunt, with eyes like black pits. It was looking right at me. And it smiled. I don’t remember standing up. I don’t remember running. I just remember the cold air burning my lungs as I scrambled down the mound, Astrid’s frantic footsteps behind me. We didn’t stop until we were back in the glow of the village’s single streetlight, bent over, gasping. We never spoke of it again. Astrid’s “midnight games” stopped. A week later, Elsa fell down the stairs at school and broke her arm. It was an accident, everyone said. Just a clumsy accident. But I knew. We had sat out on that mound. We had opened a door, not for knowledge, but out of teenage boredom and a desire for power. And something had answered. It had taken our offering of petty jealousy and given us a glimpse of the cold, hungry attention that waits in the places we’ve forgotten. The mist, I learned that night, doesn’t just cling to the edges of things. Sometimes, it has a face. And it remembers yours.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece adheres closely to the brief: rural Norrbotten, mid-90s implied, teenage Stockholm transplant Linnea, Astrid's matter-of-fact ritual instructions mixing rebellion with specific traditional elements (klok kvinna, myrk, iron nail, juniper, grounding stone), and a single midnight excursion on a burial mound. The frame as present-day recollection is handled lightly, as requested. Length is on target. Strengths: The ritual preparation sequence is the best section—Astrid's shopping-list tone against genuinely eerie specifics ("No talking. No looking back... you don't break the circle") captures the requested mix of teenage casualness and authentic tradition. The Elsa lock-of-hair detail is a strong setup that pays off in the ambiguous "accident" ending, which lands the theme of treating ancient practices as entertainment with real consequence. Ambiguity is mostly maintained—the whispers, pressure, and mist-shapes could plausibly be suggestion and panic, though the epilogue's "But I knew" tips the scale toward the supernatural more than the prompt's ambiguity strictly required. Weaknesses: The prose leans on stock horror phrases—"my blood ran cold," "a chill," "I wanted to scream"—and some images are clichéd (eyes like black pits, the smiling face in the fog). The escalation is paced well but the climax resolves abruptly; the running-away is compressed into two sentences and the emotional aftermath is summarized rather than dramatized. The final paragraph over-explains the theme ("We had opened a door... out of teenage boredom and a desire for power"), telling what the events had already shown. Astrid is vivid but thin—her "satisfied smile" when Elsa's name is spoken is the one genuinely unsettling character beat, and it deserved more development. Linnea's parents are sketched in a single line of stock imagery (father's forced cheerfulness, mother's quiet sighs). Dialogue is minimal and functional rather than weak, but Astrid's lines occasionally tilt toward exposition ("Sitting out... on a place of the old dead"). The voice is consistent—retrospective, restrained, slightly literary—and the piece is coherent and never meanders. It is engaging and atmospheric, but it plays familiar folk-horror beats (the mound, the offering, the thing that answers) without subverting them, which caps its originality. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 69.8
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The scent of lavender is a lie. It’s a soft, floral deception pumped into the sterile air, a pathetic attempt to make this room something other than what it is: a butcher’s shop where the meat is already ruined. I’m lying on my back on the vinyl-padded table, the paper crinkling under my sweatpants with every shallow breath. My left knee is a swollen, angry knot of scar tissue and shattered ambition. It throbs with a dull, metronomic pulse that has become the new rhythm of my life. The door opens, and the lie deepens. It’s him. Liam. He was there the day my ACL, MCL, and meniscus decided to stage a mutiny. We were on the same training squad, two hyper-competitive bastards pushing each other towards a finish line that, for him, has simply moved. He traded his sprint spikes for a physiotherapy degree. I traded mine for a hospital gown and a permanent limp. “Ready, Alex?” His voice is calm, professional. It’s the same voice that used to taunt me into one last, lung-burning interval. Now it’s the soundtrack to my humiliation. He’s unnervingly handsome, the kind of lean, functional fitness that looks effortless. His forearms, corded with muscle, are exposed by his short-sleeved polo. I hate that I notice. I hate that the memory of those arms driving him past me on the track is tangled up with the sight of them now, about to catalogue the wreckage of my body. “Let’s just get it over with,” I mutter, staring at the acoustic tile ceiling. He starts with the quad set. “Contract your thigh muscle, trying to press the back of your knee into the table.” I do. A pathetic, trembling fire ignites in the muscle. It’s a ghost of the explosive power I used to command. He places his hand flat on my quad, just above the kneecap. His touch is firm, clinical. But his palm is warm, and I can feel the fine, calloused texture of his skin through the thin fabric of my sweats. My breath hitches. I tell myself it’s from the effort. “Good. Hold it. Five seconds.” His fingers press slightly, assessing the contraction. It’s a professional touch, but my body doesn’t get the memo. A shiver, entirely unrelated to the pain, traces its way up my spine. I clench my jaw, focusing on the sterile white of the ceiling, on the faint hum of the air conditioner, on anything but the heat of his hand and the ghost of what we used to be. “Relax.” He removes his hand. The air feels cold where his touch was. “Now, we’ll work on range of motion.” He moves to the foot of the table, his presence a solid block at the edge of my vision. “I’m going to flex your foot, bringing your toes towards your shin.” His hands wrap around my foot. One cups my heel, the other rests on the top of my foot. It’s an impersonal hold, the kind a coach might use to demonstrate a stretch. But the intimacy of it is staggering. He’s cradling a part of me, controlling it. “Tell me when you feel a stretch.” He begins to press. The sensation is immediate—a deep, pulling tightness that snakes up the front of my shin, bypassing the main injury but reminding every other muscle that they’re under new, tyrannical management. It’s not sharp pain, not yet. It’s a warning. A threshold. “There,” I gasp, a little too quickly. He holds the position. His eyes are on my face, gauging my reaction. I can feel his gaze like a physical weight. “Breathe through it, Alex. Don’t fight it.” I try. I inhale the fake lavender, and on the exhale, I feel the muscle surrender a millimeter. He pushes a fraction further. The stretch deepens, a hot wire of tension from ankle to knee. A low groan escapes me, involuntary and raw. It sounds like something else entirely, and the silence that follows is charged. His thumbs press into the arch of my foot, a small, circular motion meant to release tension. It feels devastatingly tender. “Okay,” he says, his voice a little rougher. He releases my foot. He moves up the table, his hip brushing against my side. The contact is fleeting, accidental, but it sends a jolt through me that has nothing to do with my knee. He’s so close I can smell the clean, masculine scent of his skin, a stark contrast to the medicinal air. “Last one. A gentle passive stretch for the hamstring.” He lifts my right leg, the good one, bending my knee and bringing my thigh towards my chest. His one hand is on my hamstring, the other bracing my calf. He’s leaning over me, his face inches from mine. I can see the faint scar above his eyebrow from a fall we took on a wet track years ago. My own breath is coming in shallow pants. “Just relax your leg into my hands,” he murmurs. I do, surrendering the weight of my limb to him. He guides it, extending the knee slowly, until I feel the familiar, deep pull in the back of my thigh. It’s a clean, honest pain. The pain of a muscle being stretched to its limit. I watch his face, the focused line of his brow, the slight part of his lips. Is his breath as uneven as mine? He holds the stretch, his eyes locked on mine. The room is silent but for the hum of the diffuser and the frantic beat of my own heart. The lavender scent feels thick, cloying. This isn’t therapy. This is a different kind of crucible. He’s not just manipulating my muscles; he’s reawakening a part of me I’d thought had died on the track. A part that still responds to him, to his proximity, to his touch. He lowers my leg, his movements slow, deliberate. His hands linger for a second on my calf before he straightens up, putting professional distance between us again. “That’s it for today,” he says, his voice back to its neutral, clinical tone. But his eyes are dark, and he doesn’t quite meet my gaze. He turns to the sink to wash his hands, and I’m left alone on the table, my body humming with a confusing symphony of pain, relief, and a terrifying, rekindled heat. The lavender is a lie, but the ache in my body is brutally, beautifully real. And so is the man who just left me breathless.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is technically competent and physically coherent: each therapeutic technique (quad set, dorsiflexion stretch, passive hamstring stretch) is anatomically precise, spatially clear, and consistently tracked. The sensory detail is strong—the lavender motif, the paper crinkle, the "hot wire of tension from ankle to knee"—and the tension between clinical touch and involuntary response is well sustained. The prose is controlled, with a consistent bitter, resentful voice threaded through the session. However, there is a significant instruction violation: the prompt specifies a female physiotherapist ("her") attracted to a male protagonist, with the protagonist's shattered identity contrasted against her successful transition. The response genderswaps this to "Liam," a male physiotherapist. This discards a core premise of the prompt, including the specified dynamic of her attraction to him. The protagonist's name (Alex) is ambiguous, but the therapist's gender is unambiguous and contrary to instructions. Beyond that, the piece is somewhat conventional in its beats: the "his voice is a little rougher," the lingering touch, the charged silence—these are familiar romance-trope moves executed competently but without surprise. The resentment arc is stated more than dramatized in the second half, where the tension overtakes the bitterness. The ending's "terrifying, rekindled heat" is earned but the final line ("so is the man who just left me breathless") tips toward the overwrought. Dialogue is functional but thin. Some metaphors ("butcher's shop where the meat is already ruined," "tyrannical management") are vivid if occasionally straining. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 74.8
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The heat in Canton didn't just hang in the air; it pressed against the skin like a wet, heavy wool blanket. It was barely ten in the morning, but the sweat had already soaked through the collar of my tunic, the red wool chafing a raw line against my neck. I stepped over a pile of refuse—a rotting heap of fish heads and mangoes, their sweet, cloying decay mixing with the sharp tang of night soil. It was the perfume of the Thirteen Factories district, a smell I had once found revolting but now found merely... atmospheric. "Merrick! Hold a moment." I froze, my hand instinctively dropping to the hilt of my saber, though I hadn't the strength to draw it. I turned to see Hastings, a fresh-faced Lieutenant from the *HMS Volage*, striding toward me. His uniform was immaculate, his brass buttons gleaming in the harsh sun. "Hastings," I croaked. I cleared my throat, trying to summon the voice of an officer. "Good morning." "Damnable heat, isn't it?" Hastings wiped his brow. "Captain Elliot is looking for you. Something about the manifests for the tea shipments. He says you’ve been... elusive." "Merely inspecting the perimeter," I lied. The lie felt smooth, practiced, like a coin worn thin by constant handling. "The locals are restless. One must show the flag." Hastings frowned, his eyes narrowing as he looked me over. I knew what he saw: the tremor in my left hand, the yellowish tint to the whites of my eyes, the way my uniform hung loose on a frame that had been robust six months ago. "Right," he said slowly. "Well, don't be late for the evening muster. The Commodore is in a foul mood." "Wouldn't miss it for the world," I said, offering a salute that felt more like a flinch. He turned and marched away, the sound of his boots rhythmic and authoritative. I waited until he rounded the corner before I exhaled, a long, shuddering breath that rattled in my chest. The itch was back, crawling up my spine, whispering that time was wasting. I ducked into a narrow alleyway, leaving the European quarter behind. The architecture shifted from Western brick to the chaotic, overhanging timber of the Chinese city. I needed coin. My pay had been spent three weeks ago. I found Tommy "The Gutter" sitting on a crate near the docks, whittling a piece of driftwood. He was a deserter from the merchant marine, a man who lived in the cracks of the city. "You look peaky, Lieutenant," Tommy said, not looking up from his knife. "I need work, Tommy." "Work?" He laughed, a dry, hacking sound. "You’re a King’s man. You don’t do *work*. You do duty." "I need money," I snapped, the desperation sharpening my tone. Tommy stopped whittling. He looked at me with eyes that held no judgment, only commerce. "There’s a crate. Warehouse 4. Needs to... disappear before the customs inspector arrives. It’s marked as cotton, but it’s Indian silk. High grade." "Where does it go?" "Sampan at the end of the pier. A woman named Ah-Ming will be waiting. You get the crate to her, she gives you a cut. Enough for a month’s supply, if you’re careful." "I’m never careful," I muttered. "Then you’d better be fast," Tommy said, returning to his wood. "Clock’s ticking, James." The labor was brutal. The crate was heavy, and my muscles screamed in protest. I bribed a dock guard with a silver watch I’d stolen from a sleeping ensign last week, and I hauled the crate through the maze of sampans. The sun beat down, blurring my vision. I didn't see the woman, Ah-Ming, at first—she was just a shadow against the hull of a boat. "Tommy sent me," I grunted, dropping the crate. She inspected the goods with long, elegant fingers, then tossed a small, heavy purse at my feet. It clinked. Silver. "Go," she said in pidgin English. "You smell like a dead man." I didn't argue. I clutched the purse and fled, my heart hammering a frantic rhythm against my ribs. *The dragon is hungry,* it beat. *Feed the dragon.* I found my way to the back room of a tea house near the Creek. It wasn't the opium palace of the novels—no velvet cushions, no dancing girls. It was a damp, stone room filled with the acrid smoke of cheap tobacco and the sweet, heavy scent of boiling opium. Lao Chen sat behind a low table, a pipe in his hand. He was ancient, his face a map of wrinkles. "Lieutenant," he rasped. "You are early today." "I have money." I threw the purse onto the table. Silver coins scattered. Lao Chen didn't touch the money. He looked at me, his eyes dark and knowing. "You are burning, James. The fire inside you, it consumes the host." "I just need the smoke, Chen. Don't philosophize." "Philosophy is all we have when the flesh fails," he said softly. He reached beneath the table and produced a small, lacquered box. He opened it. Inside lay the black, treacly paste. "Three balls. That is what your silver buys." "Give me five," I rasped. "I’ll bring more tomorrow." "Tomorrow you will be sick," he said. "Three." I didn't have the strength to argue. I took the box and retreated to a shadowed corner, sinking onto a dirty mat. My hands were shaking so violently I could barely prepare the pipe. The bamboo felt heavy, alien. I held the flame to the opium. It bubbled, hissing like a living thing. I drew the smoke in. It was not a gentle relief. It was a violent, crashing wave that slammed into the back of my skull. The rotting mangoes, the heat, the memory of Hastings’s judgmental eyes, the weight of the silk crate, the shame of the uniform I wore—it all dissolved. The sharp edges of the world were sanded down into a smooth, velvet darkness. I exhaled, a plume of blue-grey smoke curling toward the ceiling. For a moment, I was not Lieutenant James Merrick, disgrace to the Royal Navy. I was just a body, floating in a warm, dark sea. The dragon coiled around my spine, purring, satisfied. But as the initial rush faded, the reality seeped back in, cold and sharp. I had to be back at the ship by six bells. I had to face Elliot. I had to scrub the grime from my fingernails and pretend I was a man of honor. I took another drag, pushing the thought away. Just one more hour. Just one more hour of peace before the tide pulls me back under.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, professional slice-of-life chapter that fulfills the brief: first person, past tense, a single day, dialogue-driven, Canton 1830s, sensory detail throughout. The sensory grounding is a genuine strength—the rotting mangoes and night soil, the chafing wool tunic, the acrid back room of the tea house. The setting feels researched rather than generic, and the choice to demystify the opium den ("It wasn't the opium palace of the novels") is a smart, self-aware touch. Character work is serviceable but thin. Merrick's desperation is well conveyed through physical tells (tremor, yellowed eyes, loose uniform), and the Hastings encounter efficiently establishes his double life. However, the supporting cast skews archetypal: Tommy "The Gutter" is a stock fixer, Lao Chen a stock sage-dealer whose "philosophy" lines ("The fire inside you, it consumes the host") flirt with fortune-cookie cliché. Ah-Ming gets one memorable line and vanishes. The dialogue is functional and occasionally sharp ("You're a King's man. You don't do work. You do duty"), but rarely surprising; exchanges resolve exactly as expected. The plot is a straightforward loop: dodge duty, get money, buy drugs, smoke. That's appropriate to the brief, but the smuggling errand resolves without friction—no complication, no cost beyond labor—so the middle sags slightly and the stakes never escalate. The "dragon" metaphor is used twice and is the most well-worn trope in addiction fiction; the piece leans on it rather than finding a fresher image. Prose is clean and controlled, with good rhythm and a few strong similes ("a coin worn thin by constant handling"). It occasionally tips into over-explanation—"The itch was back, crawling up my spine, whispering that time was wasting" tells us what we already grasp. The ending is appropriately bleak and honest, avoiding both redemption arc and moralizing, which earns its darkness. Overall: a solid, readable, well-crafted genre piece that never quite transcends its familiar beats. + Humour: Sisyphus Gives Advice — Score: 82.0
Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The morning air on the slopes of Tartarus was, as always, thick with the scent of ozone and existential dread. Sisyphus, his sandals worn thin as promises, gave the boulder a final, companionable pat before it began its familiar, sullen roll back down the hill. “Right,” he said, wiping his hands on his chiton. “Crow! The post!” A large, glossy raven descended, dropping a leather satchel onto a flat rock that served as a desk. Crow landed beside it with a theatrical ruffle of feathers. “Morning,” Crow croaked, his voice like gravel in a cement mixer. “Got the usual. A few ‘how to find your passion’ ones, a real corker about a mother-in-law, and… oh, this one’s just a smudge.” Sisyphus settled onto another rock, the boulder’s slow descent a familiar, rhythmic sigh in the background. He picked up the first scroll. *Dear Sisyphus,* *My wife says I don’t listen to her. Or something. I wasn’t really paying attention. The point is, she’s always nagging me about taking out the rubbish or fixing the squeaky gate. I feel like I’m being ground down. How do I make her see that I’m a complex individual with my own needs?* *Yours,* *Philosophically Miffed in Megara* Sisyphus chuckled, a warm, rumbling sound. “Crow, take this down. ‘Dear Miffed. She doesn’t want you to fix the gate. She wants to know you heard the squeak. The problem isn’t the gate, it’s the silence where your acknowledgement should be. Next time she mentions it, don’t say ‘I’ll do it later.’ Say, ‘That squeak is awful, isn’t it? It would drive me mad too. I’ll get the oil on Saturday.’ You’ll find the nagging transforms into a shared project. And for pity’s sake, take out the rubbish. It’s not a philosophical statement; it’s rotting vegetables. Yours, Sisyphus.’” Crow’s quill scratched. “Good one. No boulder metaphors. Subtle.” “Metaphors are lazy, Crow. People don’t want poetry; they want a plan.” He reached for the next letter, a fine parchment that smelled faintly of expensive perfume. *Sisyphus, my darling,* *I find myself in a most dreadful tangle. I am betrothed to a wonderful man—a minor deity of harbours and safe anchorage—but I have developed a passionate, all-consuming infatuation with a nymph who tends the wild roses in the eastern meadow. My heart is a ship caught between a safe harbour and a thrilling, thorny shore! What is a girl to do?* *Torn in Thrace* “Hmm,” Sisyphus mused, watching his boulder catch on a stubborn outcrop halfway down. “Crow, note the response. ‘Dear Torn. You are not a ship. You are a person with agency. The harbour is not ‘safe’ if you are dreaming of thorns, and the roses will lose their charm if you are constantly worrying about the lack of a proper mooring. My advice is this: be honest with the harbourmaster. Not about the nymph, necessarily, but about the fact that your ship yearns for different waters. It will be a difficult conversation, but it is the only one that matters. You cannot love two things fully by halves. Choose, and then commit to that choice with your whole heart. Otherwise, you will spend your life being a very well-moored, very miserable boat. S.’” “Bit nautical,” Crow observed. “She started it.” The next scroll was brittle and smelled of old cheese. *Dear Sisyphus,* *My colleague at the pottery stall, Glaukos, is insufferable. He steals my best terracotta, tells customers his glaze is superior, and once, I am certain, he replaced my finest amphora with a slightly wonky one of his own. My blood boils! How do I deal with this man without resorting to violence (which is frowned upon in the agora)?* *Fuming in Corinth* Sisyphus nodded sagely. “Ah, Glaukos. Crow, reply. ‘Dear Fuming. You cannot control Glaukos. You can only control your reaction to him. Do not compete on his terms. Instead, become undeniable. Focus on making your pottery so good, so uniquely *yours*, that his thefts and tricks become irrelevant. Let him have the wonky amphora. You make the one that people talk about for generations. Your excellence is your revenge. And document everything. Dates, times, missing pots. Present it calmly to the market overseer. Anger is a hot coal; you are the one getting burned. S.’” He stood, stretched, and began the long walk down. The boulder was waiting at the bottom, patient as a debt. As he put his shoulder to it, the familiar, solid weight settled into him. Up they went. At the summit, Crow had the final letter ready. It was a mess—a piece of cheap papyrus, the ink badly smudged by what looked like a tear or a spilled drink. “Can’t make head nor tail of this one,” Crow said, peering at it. “Looks like… ‘My… *something*… is too… *smudge*… and my… *blob*… won’t… *inkblot*.’ Could be anything.” Sisyphus took the smudged letter, holding it up to the grim, eternal light. He squinted. “No, look. The pressure of the hand here… this isn’t anger. It’s despair. And this word isn’t ‘blob,’ it’s ‘heart.’ ‘My heart won’t…’ stop? start? Let’s see… Ah! ‘My *world* is too small, and my heart won’t *fit* in it anymore.’” He looked at Crow, his eyes kind. “We know this one, old friend. Take this down. ‘Dear Friend. Your world feels small because you are looking at its walls. Your heart is growing, and that is a wonderful, terrifying thing. Do not try to shrink your heart to fit the room. Start by knocking on one of the walls. Learn a new skill. Speak to a stranger. Walk a different road. The world does not expand on its own; it expands when you push against it. Gently, but persistently. You are not trapped. You are just standing still. Start moving. S.’” Crow finished writing. “That’s… rather good.” “It’s what I would have wanted to hear,” Sisyphus said softly. He looked down the hill. His boulder was already at the bottom, waiting. “Right. Back to it.” He began the descent, not with a sigh, but with the steady, purposeful tread of a man who has found, against all odds, a second, very particular, kind of work. Crow took the finished scrolls in his beak and took flight, a dark speck against the red sky, carrying the small, fixable problems of the living world up and away.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong execution of a demanding brief. It hits nearly every constraint: epistolary format with scene-setting interjections, warm and grounded Sisyphus who is a natural at advice-giving (no fish-out-of-water flailing), genuinely practical and insightful advice, understated humor emerging from the letters themselves, and exactly one sneaked boulder-adjacent metaphor ("it expands when you push against it" — subtle enough to satisfy the constraint). The smudged-letter finale is the best structural choice: it shows Sisyphus's empathy through forensic reading of a damaged letter rather than telling us he cares, and "It's what I would have wanted to hear" is a quietly earned emotional beat. The advice itself is genuinely good — the "gate squeak" answer about acknowledgment vs. tasks, and the "well-moored, very miserable boat" line are the kind of practical wisdom the prompt requested. The letters span mundane (rubbish, pottery rivalry) to risque (the betrothed-to-a-deity infatuated-with-a-nymph letter), fulfilling the tonal range. Weaknesses: The Pratchett voice is only intermittently present. There are flashes ("sandals worn thin as promises," "patient as a debt," Crow's "gravel in a cement mixer") but the prose lacks Pratchett's characteristic digressive footnote-energy and escalating absurdity; it reads more like competent pastiche than full immersion. Crow's line "Good one. No boulder metaphors. Subtle" is a meta-wink that breaks the show-don't-tell rule the prompt emphasized — the piece comments on its own restraint, which is exactly the kind of forced self-awareness the brief warned against. The smudged-letter decoding is slightly convenient (inferring "world" and "fit" from inkblots strains plausibility, though it's charming enough to mostly get away with). The ending's "second, very particular, kind of work" edges toward telling rather than showing, though the final image of Crow carrying "the small, fixable problems of the living world" redeems it with a lovely closing image. Character consistency is excellent: Sisyphus never becomes bitter, never lectures on stoicism, and his zen quality is demonstrated through behavior (companionable pat on the boulder, purposeful tread). Crow is a functional sidekick with personality. No meandering; the piece is tight at roughly the requested length.
